maintopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING ON THE OCCASION OF HIS ARRIVAL IN CANADA

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING ON THE OCCASION OF HIS ARRIVAL IN CANADA
speechtext:
Throughout the present week his majesty's subjects in all parts of the empire have been following with intense interest and with some moments of anxiety the voyage of their king and queen across the Atlantic from the old world to the new. On Saturday, the sixth instant, the Empress of Australia weighed anchor at Portsmouth and on Tuesday next is expected to drop anchor at Wolfe's cove, Quebec. As the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) pointed out a day or two ago, on the eve of the departure of their majesties from Portsmouth the houses of parliament at Westminster passed resolutions of loyal assurance of the affectionate interest with which both houses would follow their majesties' visit to Canada and to the
Royal Visit

United States. I agree with my hon. friend that it is most appropriate that the houses of parliament at Ottawa should pass similar resolutions to greet their majesties upon their arrival at Quebec, and I have therefore the honour to present the following motion, which will be seconded by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition:
That a humble address be presented to Hia Majesty the King, conveying to his majesty, on the occasion of his arrival in Canada, assurance of the loyal affection of this house and of the eager anticipation with which it looks forward to the presence of His Majesty and of Her Majesty the Queen in this country, and of the deep interest with which its members will follow the visit of their majesties to the several provinces and to the United States.
Hon. members will be quick to recognize that, except for the application of its wording to Canada instead of to the United Kingdom, the resolution follows very much the same language, in fact almost the identical language, of the resolutions which were passed at Westminster. I mention this feature as significant because it serves to illustrate the similarity of our political institutions and also to indicate how completely the crown symbolizes the unity of the great commonwealth of nations which is also referred to as the British empire. It illustrates as well the imporant part which the personality and character of the sovereign plays in coordinating the political relations of all parts of the commonwealth.
I need not say how greatly the people of Canada will rejoice at having the honour of welcoming in person their king and queen upon the soil of Canada itself. We are deeply conscious of how considerate their majesties have been of the wishes of their subjects in Canada in arranging to come to the dominion within two years of their coronation and in making the Dominion of Canada the first of the dominions to be honoured by their presence.
It is deeply gratifying that their majesties tour will embrace all the provinces of Canada. We are grateful that the king and queen have been prepared to assume so many onerous obligations in their desire to see as much as possible of Canada and its people. I have no doubt it will be the wish of all Canadians not only that they themselves should have as large an opportunity as possible of seeing the king and queen and giving expression to their feelings of loyalty and affection, but that their majesties should have some opportunity, in addition to receiving the welcome they will in the towns and cities visited, of seeing something of the natural beauty of our country, its varied scenery, its national parks, its countryside and its peaceful homes.

We of the Commons feel particularly honoured that His Majesty the King, by graciously consenting to give royal assent to certain bills, has afforded to hon. members of both houses the opportunity of meeting with the king in parliament assembled.
It will also be pleasing to the citizens of Canada that the king and queen should have decided while visiting Canada also to pay a visit to our good neighbour to the south. I venture to say there is nothing in the course of their visit across the sea which will appeal more to the king and queen than what they will witness of the exceptionally happy relations which exist between Canada and the United States. The example of international friendship and goodwill which the countries of this continent afford is particularly significant in these days.
Before concluding I should like to express a word of appreciation of the work performed by the interdepartmental committee in making the arrangements for their majesties' visit. As the house is aware, these arrangements have been in the hands of members of the public service in the different departments in Ottawa. They have had the very helpful cooperation of officials in the different provincial capitals, and of many municipalities. On behalf of the government I wish to express our appreciation of these efforts to those who have worked so hard and cooperated so effectively in making the visit of the king and queen to our country the very memorable and historic one which we all know it will be.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING ON THE OCCASION OF HIS ARRIVAL IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have very great pleasure indeed in seconding the motion proposed by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), extending, as it does, a hearty and loyal welcome to their majesties on their first setting foot on the soil of Canada at the city of Quebec.
We Canadians are happy in belonging to the British empire and in possessing at the same time a royal family of whom we may well be proud. When I speak of the empire the word brings to my mind not only the great democracy which we call Britain-not only one-quarter of the surface of the earth and one-quarter of its population, not only that group of autonomous nations equal in status, freely associated by long friendship and ideals-but the fact that we are all united by a common allegiance to the crown; for it is the tie that binds us together.
Our empire has been blessed with many great sovereigns. My own life stretches from the great Victoria to the present ideal king- both of them constitutional monarchs, acting always on the advice of their ministers.

Electoral Matters
Among our greatest sovereigns was the father of the present king, George V, with whom was associated the beloved Queen Mary. George V did much to help foster international understanding, particularly in Tegard to the American republic, whose people learned from him much of British ideals, aims and aspirations. I join with the remark of the Prime Minister in that regard, that the visit of the present king and queen to the United States will continue to build up these fine relations existing to-day between the American republic and the British empire.
The last Christmas message of King George Y, to which we all listened with reverent affection, struck a human note which was , heard around the world; and now his son George VI is following his father's noble example.
King George VI shows the same type of greatness as that possessed by his father-a greatness displayed not in dazzling qualities but by the possession of a well-balanced mind, sound common sense, good judgment, and intense devotion to duty, combined with human understanding, sympathy for the less fortunate and downtrodden, charity for weaknesses in others, and a strong desire for peace and goodwill among the nations of the world. That is a combination of qualities rarely found in any one man.
Finally, King George VI and his gracious consort show us a noble example of home life, of happy domesticity, something for which we may be truly grateful, since the home is the very cornerstone of the nation.
For all these reasons we, the representatives of the people here assembled, whether of English-speaking or French-speaking extraction, join with one voice, one heart and one mind in welcoming His Majesty King George VI and his gracious queen to the shores of Canada. We express at the same time our fervent hope that their visit may be happy and profitable in every way and that they may return to their home in the British Isles confident of the sincere loyalty and deep affection of every true Canadian.

I wish to ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) based on a telegram which I received a short time ago. The telegram reads:
A. J. Brooks, M.P., House of Commons, Ottawa.
Hartland, N.B.,
May 12, 1939.
American potatoes being loaded at St. Leonard, Grand Falls, other points shipped under Maritime Freight Rates Act to Canadian points, otherwise Canadian taxpayer paying railway five cents hundred bonus on American potatoes, which are making loss to our growers of thousands of dollars.
H. H. Hatfield.
I would ask the minister if this matter has been brought to his attention, and if so what action he proposes to take to prevent this abuse of the privilege which belongs solely to our own people. fMr. Manion]

speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: UNITED STATES POTATOES SHIPPED INTO CANADA UNDER ADVANTAGES OF MARITIME FREIGHT RATES ACT
speechtext: The first intimation I had that this was taking place reached me through my hon. friend a very few minutes ago. I have had no opportunity as yet of making any inquiry. I have no reason to doubt that these potatoes may be entering from the United States at points near the Canadian border and are being shipped further west under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. I might point out to him that the Maritime Freight Rates Act was enacted at the request of the people of the maritime provinces in order to give them an advantage. If it is being used in this way to effect the importation and sale of foreign goods, that would be unfortunate. Perhaps my colleague the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) could say whether the benefits of the act are supposed to be extended to goods of foreign origin; I do not know. All I can say at the moment is that I shall make inquiry regarding the whole matter.

Mr. Chairman, I just wish to add a few observations to those which I offered two years ago and again last year when parliament was called upon to vote millions for so-called national defence. I then objected to any considerable increase in our military appropriations, suspecting that the armaments they were intended for would be used at the first opportunity in an extra-territorial war.
Last year, particularly, I warned the government that so long as the Canadian Militia Act did not specify the boundaries of Canada,
I would be unable to believe that the millions voted for armaments would be used solely for the defence of Canada, but would rather imagine that they were intended for the equipment of an expeditionary force to be used in any war in which England happened to be engaged for the defence of her financial and industrial interests extending to almost the entire world.
With nearly all my colleagues from the province of Quebec and many members from other provinces, I declared myself irrevocably opposed to Canada's participation in external wars.
Statement has followed upon statement, both in the house and outside the house that the millions spent in Canada for armaments would serve only for the defence of Canada and of her citizens. But this year, when the government is asking parliament to vote military appropriations surpassing anything that has been known in our history, statesmen are telling us that Canada is not a sovereign nation, that we cannot remain neutral in a war in which England is involved.
But, Mr. Chairman, if Canada cannot remain neutral in a war in which England is

Supply-National Defence
involved it logically follows that there will be participation. Would this participation take the form of the sending of contingents? Would' these contingents leave Canada in civilian attire and unarmed? It seems to me that Canada is preparing to repeat the adventure of 1914. with the sole difference that this time she will have spent a few hundred millions in advance.
Let us reason out as logically as possible the consequences of this first stage of our participation. Should contingents of volunteers be sent overseas for the defence of England, of her interests, her freedom, and so on, our soldiers, whose bravery is well known, would be targets for the enemy as they were in Flanders in 1915. The means of ^ destruction used in modern warfare will quickly thin out their ranks. Reinforcements will then be required and voluntary enlistment will no longer suffice. And, as the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) so aptly said in this house a few weeks ago, circumstances and events will prove stronger than men's wills. Conscription will inevitably be established, as it was in 1917, to the well known imperialistic cry: "To save the empire we will send our last man, our last dollar, our last railroad track."
Mr. Chairman, I repeat what I said last year: Canada, our only homeland, is not more threatened with occupation by an overseas nation than it was last year or ten or twenty years ago. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) himself stated on April 26th last that there is no need for us to prepare against a major attack or an attempted invasion. Should we go to war, he said in substance, it will be at the side of other powers for the defence of what he called vital and essential principles. It is to be feared that these principles will be vital and essential for the mother country only, and not for Canada.
I am quite sure that, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said in this house, Canada will never participate in an external war unless parliament has so decided and that the present government will never impose conscription of men on the Canadian people. But there is always the possibility, even the probability, of a union government. It is precisely because of this eventuality which brought about our experience of 1917 that I now oppose the establishment of any military organization which might lead Canada first to participation and then to conscription.
"Where is Canada's frontier?" the Montreal Gazette was asking, on April 10 last, in an editorial, of which I will quote the last paragraph :	1
[Mr Crete]
Where is Canada's frontier? Canadian public opinion would have it drawn where Britain's frontier lies. Are Canadian politicians to draw it somewhere else, in some lower and meaner place, with their eyes fixed, not upon the sacred things ot national and international life, but upon a coming general election?
That the sacred interests of Mr. John Bassett's Gazette are not limited by a Canadian frontier, everybody will admit; but it will not be as readily agreed that Canadian public opinion will bow to their dictates and forget, for their sake, those of Canada. A brief survey of the opinion of our students, whether English or French speaking, even of his own subscribers or his fellow citizens of Montreal in every walk of life, would considerably abate Mr. Bassett's boldness. He would also ascertain that politicians who draw Canada's frontier at its geographical borders have more supporters than he is willing to admit, enough, at all events, surely to shatter, when the hour comes, his imperialistic dreams.
True Canadians, who have sense enough to recognize as their sole homeland the country which provides them with means of living, do not, for all that, despise democracy. They do not make light of the sacred things of national and international life. To infer the contrary from the fact that they do not draw their country's frontier thousands of miles from its actual territory, is a purely fantastic interpretation. Those Canadians cannot believe that Canada's geographical limits are too narrow or too mean for them. But they perfectly believe, and are on the verge of sincerely hoping, that men of the calibre of Mr. Bassett will immediately cross those borders, for our Canada, with its immense resources and its democratic system, does not suit them and cannot satisfy them.
For my part, Mr. Chairman, I have no hesitation in stating in this chamber that Canada is the only country for the defence of which I will allow my children to give their life.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take advantage of this opportunity to discuss some matters of general policy with relation to national defence. Something akin to consternation was experienced when we realized the government proposed almost to double defence expenditure and enter into huge commitments for the future. That consternation has been caused by a realization that Canada requires to pay a still heavier price for what has been described as an attempt to remain at peace in a world at war.

Supply-National Defence
I do not propose to take advantage of this opportunity to indulge in any abuse of the government, or any attempt to make public statements that might be construed as embarrassing to the officers in charge of our defence operations. But I must point out that we are confronted with a defence problem, with plans for warlike measures on the part of a peace loving people, because we live in a world that is now governed by anarchy and balance-of-power politics. I do not propose to reopen the discussion of international affairs or Canada's foreign policy. I am bound however to say at this juncture that our foreign policy should shape our defence policy. There is little in our foreign policy as declared by the government that enables any clear definition of strategical objectives in our defence expenditures.
Reviewing the statements of policy made by the government, and the review made only the other day by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), I think it must be realized that at this time we are displaying a far greater interest in the measures that must be taken after war breaks out than in those steps which might be attempted even in the right of Canada to avoid entanglement in a war. We have made very little effort to establish any moral principle either in our diplomatic or in our trading relationships, and I submit that there is consequently little sense of direction in our defence plans.
Our chief weakness in this respect has been very well described by Professor A. R. M. Lower in a recent article appearing in the current issue of the Canadian Forum. Professor Lower cannot in any sense be described as an opponent of defence measures. In my opinion his contributions to discussions of defence problems in Canada have been most outstanding and realistic. He has this to say by way of preface to his views on Canadian defence:
During the crushing series of defeats that Germany has been administering to France and England, this country literally has had no foreign policy. It has been a waiter upon events. Nothing could be more humiliating to those who have an affection for their native land than the way in which the majority of people wobble about, without will or decision of their own, taking their lead from a distant statesman over whom they have no control, who has no responsibility towards them, whose policy they cannot influence in any particular, for whom, or against whom, they cannot even vote.
And, the writer cannot forbear to add, a statesman with whose policy the majority of English speaking Canadians if they understood it (which of course they do not), would find themselves in sharp disagreement. ... Yet, even now, with all that has happened, of real understanding of our interests, as opposed to sentimental ancestor-worship, there is, except 71492-253
on the part of a small group, little sign. We were and are a nation of "Yes-men," a squad of infantry changing our dire tion in unthinking obedience to the commands of the sergeant-major across the water. And worse still, a sergeant-major who is not even aware that he is ordering us about.
That must not continue to happen. Taking our cue from statesmen of older countries we must decide what Canada's vital national interests are. The decision must be taken neither narrowly or sentimentally.
Professor Lower then goes on to enumerate the things which in his opinion we as Canadians must do to defend ourselves in the new kind of world into which we are entering, a world in which we must depend largely on ourselves, as was pointed out last night by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey).

However, in a discussion of the defence program we have no alternative but to start from the position in which we have been placed by the attitude taken by the government. I propose this afternoon to deal with the matter, not theoretically but so far as I may from the common sense point of view, and from the distinctly Canadian point of view which it is essential we should hold at this time. I have in mind the words of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), uttered only a few days ago, in which he expressed the view that sentiment is an unsafe basis upon which to make a decision. I see no reason, under the circumstances, why we should approach this problem in a state of jitters, or why we should resort to emotional outbursts. We should take the common sense, realistic approach to the problem and attempt to work it out as practical men.
I must point out at this stage, however, that there are fundamental considerations with which we have not come to grips, fundamental considerations which some day we must face if we are to deal effectively with problems of war. At the moment I must pass on from those considerations to the more immediate and practical problems presented in the minister's outline, at the same time emphasizing the fact that if we are to escape the horrors of war we must deal with the causes of war more effectively than we have dealt with them in the past.
At the moment the minister has placed before us an immediate and practical problem, namely that of reviewing a particular program of expenditures for purposes of defence. And because of the startling increase in the expenditures for the defence program our responsibilities are greater than ever before,

and we cannot discharge those responsibilities by a casual or desultory discussion of the problem. In his statement the minister has brought us to the point where, as members of the House of Commons we must come to close grips with the problem and give these expenditures detailed study. He states that the defence program or at least the expenditures contained in these estimates, have been the result of the government's appraisal, not only of the relevant aspects of the policy with respect to external affairs, but also of the risks apprehended and the equipment and forces required to cope with such risks. Since we last discussed defence estimates in this house certain factors in the international scene have become more apparent, and these have a definite bearing on our defence problem. I propose to enumerate the more important factors, some of which, while always present, have become more apparent.
First, the axis powers have more openly and more defiantly declared their intention to employ war or the threat of war in order to subdue or dominate other nations. Second, within the last month there has been a complete reversal of policy on the part of the democratic powers. They are now feverishly attempting to build up by means of antiaggression pacts a substitute for the league, and this is coupled with an armament race unprecedented in its proportions. Third, Great Britain has undertaken definite military commitments on the European continent. This has now been formally announced, and that fact alone must necessarily involve a change in commonwealth defence plans. Fourth, the President of the United States has declared more definitely that hostile action against Canada will be regarded as hostile action against the United States. Fifth, statements have originated in practically all the dominions and in Great Britain that in the event of Britain being involved in war, expeditionary forces from the dominions will not be expected or desired as an effective part of the discharge of mutual obligations. Emphasis from the commonwealth point of view has been more clearly placed on the responsibility of each dominion for its own defence. Sixth, and last, it is more apparent now that the axis powers have established naval and submarine bases in Spain and in northern Africa, from which bases raids may be more effectively directed against British shipping.
No doubt these are some of the factors which have influenced the administration to provide for these defence expenditures and undertake huge commitments for the future. I submit that we should not view these estimates as being merely financial commitments.

Every commitment made in this regard involves the possible expenditure of human life. We should consider these matters as being not only financial obligations but obligations or commitments with regard to Canadian lives. Our defence policy should bear a definite relation to the realities of the situation as I have outlined it, and to our resources and geographical position. If the necessity for defence is thrust upon us, we should devise a sound, well-balanced and well-coordinated defence program adapted to meet Canada's needs. The impression left by the statement of the minister is that in the opinion of the staff nothing matters but arms. A realistic view of the situation reveals that Canada cannot safely rely for defence upon armaments alone.
Our responsibility does not end merely with the voting of these appropriations. The minister has made it clear that although much is demanded from Canada this year for defence, much more may be required in years to come. Because of the imperative need for a clearly-defined defence policy, all the implications of that policy and its bearing upon our national life should be discussed in this house at this time. It is not enough that we should merely view a dangerous situation and then hurriedly sign a larger cheque on the national treasury for defence expenditures. As far as I can judge, the larger the appropriations are for the fighting services, the less we have in the way of defence and the more they want. On each occasion that we have considered defence expenditures in recent years we have been assured that Canada will be well protected, and then this show is put on all over again.
Since we must think in terms of defence, it is our responsibility to examine the existing world situation in relation to our own safety. The greater the appropriations for defence, the greater the responsibility of parliament in this regard. We cannot accept blindly any ready-made scheme. Even where there is agreement as to the necessity of increased expenditures for defence, there still can be sincere and important differences of opinion as to policy. Until certain matters of policy are more clearly defined, we shall always have uneasiness and uncertainty throughout Canada with regard to defence. We cannot discharge our responsibilities simply by voting large sums like a lot of sheep.
I ask the government to provide a more satisfactory method for the discussion of our defence policy. I think we have reached this stage in this important question. I had intended to propose a special defence committee of the house, and I am glad the leader

I appreciate that. May I say that such a procedure would be necessary in the event of a defence emergency, and certainly it should be followed now if the dangers of the situation are so great as to involve these increased commitments. I suggest the usual reservations should be made as to military and naval secrets. Although I am intensely interested in our defence problem, I for one would not care to have the responsibility of knowing technical military or naval secrets. There need be no fear on that score. A great deal of important information was embodied in the minister's statement the other day, and after all the agents of foreign powers in Canada probably know a great deal more about defence than do members of parliament. I see no good reason why members of the house cannot be trusted to study the defence problem as they do other public issues.
Hitherto there has been a "take it or leave it" attitude on the part of the general staff and the administration. That does not make for a wholesome situation. Nothing could be more useful at this juncture than a report to the house based on the hearing of evidence from qualified technicians and the discussion of policy from all points of view. I believe there would be a most wholesome effect as a result of such discussion. There has been some justification for the articles which have recently appeared in Canadian periodicals criticizing parliament in connection with defence matters. One writer says that the members of the house usually ask the wrong questions and never get the right answers. Never at any time has there been a comprehensive survey of the whole question as a matter of public policy from all angles. I think we must all admit if we cast our mind's eye back over the discussion of defence policy in recent years that there is good ground for that criticism.
I think there is also good ground for the criticism that results are not always commensurate with the expenditures. This reaction 71492-253 i
is inevitable throughout the country when information as to policy and general plans of administrative action is disclosed only during debates largely conducted along partisan lines. A review of past years will convince any reasonable member of the house that there would have been greater confidence at this time in the Department of National Defence had there been greater frankness at the outset and throughout the years. The absurd situation exists to-day that any hon. member who criticizes or questions the defence policy as reported to the house is immediately accused of opposing defence, of disloyalty, of sabotage of national interests. I for one am not opposed to reasonable defence measures as such. I repeat what I have said before, that I believe it to be the responsibility of the government to provide defence against external danger; but when I say that, it does not bind me to agree in all matters relating to defence, nor does it prevent me from holding convictions as to what defence policy is best adapted to Canadian needs.
More than ever before, defence is a matter of vital concern to all the people, and is not merely the concern of a small official group. As far as possible, all the evidence upon which important decisions have been made should be before the house in detail. I suggest that the only way such matters can be examined in detail is by a committee of the house. In any defence emergency we shall require much more than military or naval preparedness. It will demand effective coordination of all our principal national enterprises.
A democracy is effective in defence only when public morale is at a high level. A dictatorship may move more quickly at the outset, but it cannot maintain that morale, nor can it survive any serious reverse. Canada is not in such great danger as to warrant any form of military dictatorship. I believe that for the most part we find common ground in the desire to preserve our democratic institutions, and it is very easy to destroy democratic institutions by preparing to defend ourselves in the wrong way. For that reason, I submit, our military preparations should be subject to certain controls which are an essential part of our democratic institutions. If we do not exercise those controls, if a defence program is introduced into this house with a sort of implied warning-"Hands off, or we will brand you as disloyal"-we shall not make very much progress. We must, o* course, exercise some restraint in public debate, otherwise we may be throwing crumbs of comfort to an unfriendly power. No one will deny, I think, that committee work in this

house has served a very useful purpose, even with regard to the most contentious matters. For these reasons, it seems to me, a committee of the house should be asked to give special study to this question in the light of all the circumstances.
I submit that one of the principles _ which underlie our expenditure at this time is that all defence measures should be strictly for the direct defence of Canadian shores. No appropriation should be made for any other purpose at this juncture. There should be no doubt on this matter, and there should be no unwise diffusion of effort. It has been stated authoritatively in many quarters within the commonwealth that if we do this we shall be making our maximum contribution as a Canadian people towards collaboration with friendly nations. If we do this job thoroughly we shall be taxing all our resources. We cannot do it thoroughly if we attempt to imitate the preparations of first-class powers. It is clear as never before that Canadian defence must be planned and carried on solely with reference to Canadian conditions. The minister himself emphasized that point when he said that Canada will not be required to carry on war single-handed, but only in collaboration with first class powers. Canada is not a first-class power, nor should we pretend that we are, or make provisions in the estimates on the assumption that we can carry out the motions of a first-class power. By that I mean that we cannot hope as a nation to develop a striking force which might injure or destroy enemy forces before they reach our shores. It is in vain to suppose that we could provide, for instance, a battle fleet which might engage and destroy at sea the raiding forces of a first-class naval power. We should concentrate at this juncture on placing our own shores in a proper state of defence, to the exclusion of all other considerations.
In some quarters it is contended that we should throw our whole weight into the battle on other frontiers and thus gain the advantage of the indirect defence of Canada. Such a policy might well prove to be national selfdestruction. We shall do well if we make ready to defend ourselves without expecting aid from elsewhere. It is now made clear, I think, from reviewing all we know of empire plans of defence, that this is our first, and at this juncture our only, responsibility. If for sentimental reasons we attempt more ambitious schemes, we shall neglect the primary duty of national security, and that neglect will prove damaging not only to ourselves but to cooperating nations. Our own national

security should be our first concern, since it is clear that we shall be at war in collaboration with other powers. Let us not forget that such collaboration is weakened if we neglect our home defence.
The existence of large standing armies and navies in Europe or across the Pacific does not compel preparations in Canada to defend ourselves against invasion by any large foreign army. The whole question of trans-oeeanic warfare has been carefully reviewed during the past year by experts in all countries, particularly in the United States, and there is unanimity of opinion that no first-class power or combination of powers can successfully direct any hostile action resulting in seizure of territory on this continent. Military strategists in the United States, high-ranking officers of the United States forces, have computed that the maximum force which could be brought against this continent is in the neighbourhood of 200,000 combat troops. This is assuming that enemy powers could at the same time guard their own frontiers and dispatch an invading armada across the ocean without interference. With each combatant it would be necessary to transport four tons of supplies as well as eight tons of equipment. Upon this basis the transport of even
100.000	combatant troops would require
1.200.000	tons of shipping, or three-fifths of Germany's entire shipping. This is a computation based on estimates of experts in the United States. I submit that it is absurd in the extreme to speculate that any power or combination of powers would at one time mobilize a fleet of over 300 transports, with naval protection equivalent to the entire strength of the German navy, taking twelve days, as would be required in the case of merchantmen, to land an army of merely
100.000	soldiers on this continent. There are few ports where they would find the necessary equipment to unload artillery, combat tanks and munitions. They would have to tow various types of special landing devices. Of any such movements we would have ample warning. If the combined United Kingdoa and United States navies did not engage and destroy such a fleet, it is absurd to suppose that we could do anything about it, here, even with the forces we would have at our command on Canadian shores. No first-class power, however, would risk the consequences of such a venture. With our natural advantages for defence and reasonably efficient coastal defence we could repel such an invasion. We can brush aside for many years the alarms

raised by some that, at any moment, there may suddenly appear on our coasts a large raiding force.
During the period between May, 1917, and November 1, 1918, the United States moved
884,000	troops across to France on American ships. They used 802 vessels apart from the British transports. They gradually put into service another 900 vessels, but in July, 1918, they were able to transport only 300,000 men a month. They could not land more than 25,000 tons of supplies a day, although they required 40,000 tons daily to keep their armies in the field. If these are the facts of the situation, the facts we know, what then have we to fear in this respect from Japan, with only 637 ships in its entire merchant fleet, or Germany, with 2,321 ships of all kinds?
The landing of an army of any size with equipment and supplies on either coast, equipped to hold and occupy Canadian territory, can be described only as an hallucination. The alarming prospect of a battle fleet laying waste our coasts also seems to hold terrors for some. Here again we may refer to the considered opinion of experts. Admiral Sims said not long ago that "a battleship fleet is tied down to its base and has a radius of not over 2,500 miles." He ridiculed the idea that a Japanese fleet could cross the Pacific and bring with it fuel enough to reach United States shores, to manoeuvre and fight, and then return 7,000 miles to its home waters.
The opinion of leading high-ranking officers in the United States is that the offensive range of modern fleets is not above 2,500 miles. Den-linger and Gary in their "War on the Pacific" put it at 2,000 miles. There is reason to doubt that any of the new German battleships, or even the Japanese battleships, have fuel capacity to enable them to engage in battle on this side of the Atlantic. We know with certainty now, by reason of investigations made at Scapa Flow, that on account of limited fuel capacity, the German fleet during the great war could not have attacked our harbours. We well remember the warnings then broadcast of the danger that a German fleet might destroy our ports. I mention these facts to show that there is no occasion for hysteria with regard to manoeuvres of battle fleets in force off our coast.
In this connection, it is interesting to note the statement made by Lieutenant-General MacArthur with reference to the Philippines. These islands are more exposed to attack than any point in Canada, and never have American naval experts pretended that they
could protect the Philippines by waging war against the Japanese in their own waters. General MacArthur stated that, with a few more years to train the native troops, he could guarantee to hold the islands against the full force of a Japanese attack. He gave as his reason that ships' guns and planes are ineffective, even against relatively weak shore defences. As Professor Lower points out, if that can be said for a distant and vulnerable position like the Philippines, it certainly can be done all the more easily for a country as naturally strong as Canada.
The prospect of devastating air raids is not as terrifying as some would have us believe. The longest single flight made by a plane is 6.295 miles. As Major Eliot points out in his recent work, The Ramparts We Watch, acclaimed by military experts, the military radius of action is roughly about one-fourth of the maximum range; that is, the plane must go out from its base, and return, which cuts the range in half. He then states that the maximum range of a bombing plane to-day is only 1,500 miles-750 miles out and 750 miles back. Admiral Leahy, recently testifying before the congress committee on naval affairs, with reference to the fortification of Guam, stated that planes could not reach Japan proper from Guam loaded with bombs, although the distance is only 1,400 miles. The evidence goes to show that the axis powers, unlike the United States and Great Britain, have not planned aircraft construction for long range flying.
With regard to air raids on this continent, Major Eliot has this to say:
While it is theoretically possible for single planes to fly across the Atlantic with a very small military load, drop a bomb or two and return, as a practical operation of war even this is out of the question, and will remain so as far as now can be foreseen; a serious attack by a large unit is still less to be envisaged. Planes which did not expect to return might raid our coasts, but no nation has enough long-range bombers and highly trained crews to waste them in enterprises of this nature.
Another alarm has been raised on the suggestion that enemy powers might establish aircraft bases at points near our coasts, and to these bases dispatch large fleets of planes for raiding purposes. There is always the possibility that an enemy may attempt to utilize some landing field at inconvenient points, but we should not overlook the practical difficulties in the way of establishing bases for continued operations. Would it be possible to establish hangars for, say, even twenty-five planes without exposing the position to a vigilant patrol? The German detail

fifteen men to keep one plane in the air. How could a distant power maintain a base with all the necessary skilled mechanics and special machinery required? The answer is that no distant enemy power would waste men and equipment on so fruitless and costly a venture.
All reasonable calculations as to the risks confronting Canada in a world war eliminate the probability of enemy action in force. I mention these things because I am extremely suspicious when men rise and speak vaguely and in general terms of terrible dangers to which we are exposed. I wonder what they are trying to justify.
There remains only the probability of occasional hit-and-run attacks by small raiding forces of aircraft or naval forces of aircraft or naval vessels either separately or acting in combination, provided they can escape naval action on the Atlantic or the Pacific. To this may be added the possibility of submarine attacks on shipping. This is the actual risk and the outside limits of the risk to which our ports and shipping focal areas might be exposed, and then only infrequently.
As already suggested, there might be an attempt to employ the Hudson bay route during the summer season, in order to strike at vital centres in Canada. Obviously, we cannot ring these centres about with antiaircraft guns. Infantry and field artillery cannot protect cities against bombing. When we consider the actual problem, with its most dangerous limits, the answer is coastal defence. If we are vulnerable through the Hudson bay route, the obvious defence is to extend our coast patrol with air bases at suitable points, that such provision may (be made as to enable action that will close that entrance during the open season. It is not reasonable to assume that any enemy power is so well supplied with aircraft carriers at this time that it can undertake the risks of navigation to which it would be exposed and the possibility of capture that would be involved in a raid from that direction.
In the world situation outlined by the minister, it is this phase of the problem that should have priority. Any ambitious attempt by which our effort may be dissipated in other directions will mean the neglect of this primary responsibility, and ignore the known risks.
In our defence establishment, we have an intermingling of two distinct traditions. We have the colonial tradition, to which the minister has referred, and which has resulted in a string of expensive armouries across the country, an extraordinary number of unite and commands with an expenditure that is

largely waste as regards coastal defence. In many respects it is a survival of the days when we prepared to repel attacks from the south.
There is another tradition which survives from the great war, and which involves plans for an expeditionary force abroad, and the equipment and strategy of an army of manoeuvre. These two traditions are outmoded and should be abandoned for the more modern plan of devising defence as though for an island nation. All our effort in this regard should be defensive in the strict sense of the term. Under the existing circumstances we cannot risk taking the offensive even in collaboration with other powers. Any such collaboration would mean the neglect of defence, resulting in exposing a vulnerable weakness and flanking action against ourselves as well as our allies.
We should examine our naval preparations in the light of the actual requirements for coastal defence. Apparently we are to have a destroyer flotilla. What is the objective of that policy? Are we putting together some sort of Canadian navy on no plan at all, merely as circumstances press? If we are building up to the cruiser stage and intend to have a fleet, such a policy should be openly discussed and strategical objectives defined. A raiding force crossing the ocean would likely include one cruiser, carrying 6-inch or 8-inch guns. Against such ships, destroyers would be powerless. Destroyers are expensive and unnecessarily fast for convoy work. For an anti-submarine patrol, small fast ships with modem detection devices are much more effective.
Destroyer flotillas can have little useful function apart from a battle fleet. All the strictly Canadian purposes could be served more adequately and at much less expense by smaller ships. If we are thinking of Canadian vulnerability, a submarine lying in wait off the entrance to Hudson bay would prove of more value with an air patrol than all our six destroyers. Either we have no plan at all in this regard or we are actually planning the assembly of a naval unit to function as a part of the British navy. For this, the Naval Service Act provides. Our destroyer force may be serving mainly as a training school for future expansion or for graduation into the British navy. We should know in which direction we are travelling. We cannot take both courses. For defensive purposes the emphasis should be placed now on the acquisition of fast "mosquito craft," carrying torpedoes and equipped with listening devices, supported by the destroyers we already have.

We should have mine fields and booms. These would provide much more formidable defence for Canada than more destroyers or cruisers at this stage.
When the minister says our first line of defence is our air force I think he overemphasizes its importance. Aircraft are useful for patrol, "spotting" for naval guns and shore batteries. They may be used to impede a landing or bomb out bases. We know now from experience that they can do relatively little damage to approaching ships. We know also that as the speed of aircraft increases the chances of our defence squadrons intercepting and engaging a raiding squadron decrease. The air force is essentially an auxiliary arm to naval forces and coastal batteries. If the risks are those stated by the minister, the country may well ask why we are spending so much on aircraft and have so few anti-aircraft guns and fire control instruments in the country. Large orders are now being placed for searchlights, but what practical value will they have without batteries of anti-aircraft guns to fire on the planes so spotted? Obviously the program is out of balance, unless it is proposed that we dispatch our air squadrons abroad. Here again we have the dead1 hand of tradition, more British than the British-British training, wholesale cooperation with the British authorities, everything in a groove by reason of our experience in the last war, by reason of that cooperation with England. There is a tendency to neglect primary Canadian responsibilities, with results which will prove a source of danger and may prove disastrous to any form of effective cooperation with the United States or with Great Britain. The whole spirit of the force is anti-national-it is not national. There is a slavish adherence to the British system, with the result that much of our defence organization bears very little real relation to our actual needs.
I submit that we are building a force more with the design of taking the field as an army of manoeuvre rather than with a view to problems of coastal defence. We have first the system of training based on the exchange of officers with the British authorities, all based on the idea of cooperation for purposes other than the direct defence of Canadian shores-everything for the preparation of an expeditionary force. I consider that to be the general expectation of the great majority of the officers on the active list. The whole plan of organization suggests a skeleton outline of army divisions equipped according to British army specifications. If we are still
thinking of defence, we may never have to assemble an entire army division complete in all arms and units, as they do on the European continent.
It is more likely that for purposes of defence we require a highly specialized division with emphasis on the engineering services, coastal batteries, signals and anti-aircraft work. I think we may properly question the organizing of tank battalions unless we are preparing to take the field. It may be argued that tank regiments may be useful against landing parties; if so why do we not train them on the terrain on wffiich they must fight? We have too many infantry units, and many of them are over-officered. The disposition of units and commands bears no real relation to the problems of coastal defence.

I question the preponderance of field artillery. I do not suggest that we should abandon field artillery now in the possession of the department. Light and medium artillery may be required to repel landing parties principally after landing has been

made. Here again I suggest the training has not been on the terrain on which they may be required to fight. Furthermore there is no plan of highways developed to enable effective action on the part of light or medium artillery in the event that they have to deal with landing parties in force. If we are honest about the defence of our shores we must recognize that we require heavy guns, 9-2 for instance, to engage hostile ships, far more than field guns, unless we are going on some excursion abroad.
I noticed in the list prepared by the department that they are asking for howitzers and howitzer ammunition. Why howitzers instead of 6 inch or 9'2 inch guns? The howitzer is an arm used to shell enemy positions occupied in strength. Why mortars? And so on down the list submitted by the minister the other day. Apart from items for purely coastal defence, the list includes 544 infantry mortars, 60 medium howitzer equipments, 20 medium gun equipments, 500 field gun equipments, 348 anti-tank equipments; for mobile army armament, $17,000,000 and for ammunition, $17,000,000.
These questions should be answered. I may be all wrong, but as I understand the use of artillery of this sort it is for other purposes than coastal defence. It would appear that the staff have decided that we must fight abroad. I am not suggesting that the staff are conspiring against the interests or wishes of Canada, but I think they believe it likely that sentiment in Canada will demand the dispatch of an expeditionary force overseas and therefore, particularly in the light of historical precedents, they must prepare for such a contingency. They are going ahead on that basis. I submit that sentiment is an unsafe basis for such a decision. I cannot forget that at the beginning of the last war the staff was responsible for horrible blunders which cost many thousands of lives. At this time I am not going into matters which are the subject of inquiry before the public accounts committee, but we may deal with the matter of policy behind the Bren gun order.
At the outset we find the initiative was not taken by our staff. We read that it was learned that the British war office had decided that the Bren gun would be standard equipment for their forces, therefore Canada followed the example. They decided that the requirements should be 7,000 Bren guns. Now why that, when we are thinking in terms of coastal defence? The Bren gun is a light machine gun designed for use by infantry; it requires two men to operate it, it has only

thirty rounds of ammunition in the magazine; after a period of sustained lire or even after a burst at any period the barrel must be changed. It is not a weapon designed for the type of sustained fire which will be urgently required for coast defence. If I were an officer charged with the defence of a port on the coast, east or west, and had to deal with raiding forces of the type which we may expect, I should be calling for heavy .machine guns like the Vickers, capable of sustained fire, probably from a machine gun emplacement. The Bren gun would probably serve some useful purpose at various points, but certainly 3,500 on the Pacific coast and 3,500 on the Atlantic far exceed our needs for light machine guns for purposes of strictly coastal defence.
Furthermore, reports have been communicated to me from officers on active service on the frontiers of the British empire who say that the troops have thrown away the Bren gun, not because it is obsolete or defective in construction but because it is not the type of weapon required in emergencies where sustained fire is required, and 'because it requires two men to operate it, thus doubling the risk of casualties. We should know the evidence upon which such a vital decision was made, concerning a contract on the part of Canada involving commitments which may amount to $6,000,000, when we are not securing a weapon designed to meet the requirements of coastal defence. I know, from a return tabled in the house this session, that the department is securing a limited number of heavy machine guns from Great Britain, but I submit that the emphasis has been on the light machine guns instead of the heavier guns required for coastal defence.
To sum it up, the fact of the matter is that to-day we are without adequate coastal defence against those risks of which we know; the risk of armed merchantmen, the risk of raiding aircraft squadrons or cruisers able to release a few planes. That is the type of raid to which we will likely be exposed. We are not making plans to defend ourselves against these known risks, because we are attempting to follow two systems at the same time, and it cannot be done. You cannot develop skeleton plans for an expeditionary force, for an army of manoeuvre, and at the same time concentrate training forces and equipment on purely coastal defence. Even if we are to enter into any plan of collaboration with other nations, we shall be required to give first attention to Coastal defence, and I do not believe our energies and plans should be diverted from that problem now.

Supply-National Dejence
I have a word to say about an expeditionary force, because of the public statement made recently in that regard. I think that matter should be canvassed very carefully and earnestly, and perhaps a committee of this house would be the proper place to examine it.
