speechtext: Order.

Mr. Chairman, as I do not want to delay in the least the work of the house, I will not make a speech, but I wish to register, this year again, my renewed opposition to the increase in the defence appropriations. I believe that we are entering upon a dangerous armament race, and I strongly oppose that course.

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire inordinately to prolong the debates of the house. May I be permitted, however, to make certain statements and to underline certain views which appear, to my mind, to be taking root in this house,. There is current an opinion to the effect that members who oppose the defence estimates seem to lack confidence in, or to cast doubts on the good faith of their leaders. We fully acknowledged this good faith in the first speeches we made on the subject of defence estimates. In an address delivered in this house, in 1937, I stated that one could not doubt the sincerity of the men who governed Canada to-day. It is quite evident, Mr. Chairman, that even if one were to look up encyclopaedias and lexicological text-books, it would not only be impossible to prove that I am mistaken, but, on the contrary, the error of those who claim that we have lost faith in the sincerity of our leaders would become manifest. To my mind, not to share a man's opinion and to doubt his sincerity are two very different things.

Hear, hear.
[Mr. Slaght.l

I declare solemnly
that all such insinuations should cease and that we are entitled, whether we come from Quebec or elsewhere, to have differences of opinion with the Government without being pointed out as members who doubt the sincerity of their leaders. When western members vote against the budget or any other government-sponsored measure, none asserts that they doubt the sincerity of their leaders, but simply that they do not share their opinion.
It seems to me that we are entitled to exercise the same privilege, even with regard to the defence estimates.
Hear, hear.

I think I have stated
our position clearly enough so that none can misunderstand it.
It is now being claimed, and repeatedly so, that the bombardment of our cities and coasts by aircraft is the gravest danger and threat we have to face, in view of recent scientific developments, particularly in the field of aviation. I have examined the defence estimates and I have found no mention therein of the construction of shelters in which our population could take cover during an air raid. Those who observed the march of events in the Spanish conflict, are aware that Madrid was able to hold out to the end because of the shelters which protected the civilian population against aerial bombardment by the Nationalist air force, shelters wherein the people took cover and remained until the conclusion of each air raid. To my knowledge, no such shelters have been constructed for the protection of our civilian population. It is therefore evident, Mr. Chairman, that this danger of aerial bombardment, if real, is not as serious as some would have us believe. Regarding the possibility of an enemy base being established in Hudson Bay and the assertion made in this house that we should concentrate part of our defence forces in the Hudson Bay area, may I say that I entertain certain doubts, without, however, mistrusting the sincerity of its author.
Mr. Chairman, we often hear in the course of a war, or even during peace time, particularly at the approach of an armed conflict, appeals addressed to the French-Canadians, in which they are asked to consider well all the privileges granted to them by England. Now I have no desire to attack the British crown, but I feel that especially in time of peace, such appeals should not be resorted to,

Supply-National Defence
as we would not then be obliged to wage such difficult battles, at times, in order to obtain certain favours we request on behalf of our constituents. I am not making insinuations against any department head whatever, but I would speak at greater length on the subject if it were possible to do so within the limits of this debate. Still, I consider that the French-Canadians have had to struggle for all the privileges they may now enjoy, and that they have immediately paid for everything they obtained. We have but to recall the years of 1775, 1812 and 1837, to realize that "the French-Canadians have paid a good price for whatever advantages and liberties were granted to them by the British crown.
We may be blamed and charged with narrow-mindedness for opposing the defence estimates, or rather this increase in the defence estimates. In fact, there is a great difference between the two, which everyone apparently tries to ignore, for our opposition is directed solely against the increase in these estimates. It does not mean that we are opposed to national defence, as evidenced by the building of shelters for the protection of our people against air raids, which I mentioned a few moments ago. I am sure, at least, that it would be impossible to take such shelters out of the country for use in an external war. We may seem to be lacking in broadmindedness, but I recall the statement of a man whom I consider a great patriot, even though I have been charged with doubting his sincerity. I am referring to the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). He said in this house that when a French-Canadian leaves this country he does not feel that he is returning home. I fully agree with that statement. When a Liberal member or a member from any other party protests against what he considers an undue increase in the defence estimates, it is not because he is too narrow-minded. We are quite often told about the very wide extent of our country; therefore, it seems to me that those who believe in the protection of her natural boundaries should at least be considered as broadminded enough.
Mr. Chairman, we are sometimes told that certain men are fond of popular applause because they make patriotic statements; such men are even called blatant patriots. When we show our patriotism in our own way, or, if you prefer, as we understand it, I do not feel that it is any easier, in such case, to gain popular applause than in making a show of bravery, especially when the enemy is still
3,000	miles away. It may be asked of French-Canadians and of the younger generation of
Canadians, whether French or English-speaking-for I do know that many young Canadians of English extraction are opposed to Canada's participation in external wars-it may be asked of us whether we are willing to help England or the British empire. We are quite willing to do that, but we feel that we can best do it in using our man power and our resources for the sole defence of our country and only within her territory.
Hear, hear.

That is my view, and I believe there are many who agree with me. Is it sinful or criminal to believe that young Canadians should not be called upon to fight overseas? At the time the Munich agreements were signed, we began to hear appeals for the salvation of democracy, as had happened during the war of 1914-18. But had we participated in a European war at that time, on what ground would we have fought? We would have gone to war for the salvation of Czechoslovakia, a country that came into being through the treachery of Mazaryk towards the Slovaks, a treachery that was also continued by president Benes.
What did Benes say at the Versailles Conference? It would have been easy at that time to avoid carving out a country filled with countless elements of discord. However, that country was created with various nationalities and if, to-day, we were asked to fight in order that Poland might keep the German city of Danzig, could we be blamed for entertaining doubts about the advisability of our intervention? We do not doubt the sincerity of others, but we do not want our good faith to be suspected.
We claim the privilege of freely expressing our views; we are now and will continue to be liberals, because the liberal party knows no bondage and because we are entitled to our own opinions, even though they may differ from those entertained by others.
At the Versailles Conference, Mr. Benes said:
Look at this Slovak delegation. It consists mostly of Roman Catholic priests. They are sent here by the Vatican and the Hapsburgs.
How nice!
Can we blame our young Canadians for being unwilling to fight for a nation which was thus formed?
I think I have already said, and I repeat now, that I have no reason, no more than those of my opinion, to be ashamed because of our opposition to the participation of a single Canadian soldier in an external war. I remember the election campaign in which I
Supply-National Defence

fought at the side of Hon. Lucien Cannon- who is remembered in this house as a man of fairly sound judgment-when he stated on public platforms in the county of Portneuf: "Not a man, not a cent." I have no reason to change my mind, to-day. I express my opinion accordingly and I do not care if some question my sincerity and are prone to believe that I make my statement in order to secure cheap applause or victory at the next election. Man is made up of a mind and a heart. I use my mind and I let, as far as possible, my heart speak, not being convinced that I am on the wrong road.
What is the quotation?
It is from a book entitled "Reminiscences of Professor Francis Je'hlicka," a Slovak.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this subject. Before proceeding with what I have in mind, may I say that I find myself in the same position as that which I occupied last year when I followed the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier).
(Translation) As I said to my friend the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) in French last year, I do not question his sincerity but I do not share his views. I do not think the views he has expressed this morning are those of the province of Quebec or of most of his compatriots. When he was speaking of conscription there came to my mind the thought that, as we say in English, he is whipping a dead horse. I say to my hon. friend that conscription is dead and that the conscription cry should not be sounded in our province at the next elections. All the parties-Conservative, Liberal and C.C.F.-are of one mind on the subject, and I do not think the hon. member will help his cause at the coming elections in that manner. As I said in English, he is whipping a dead horse.

My hon. friend will allow me to point out to him that I do not seek by this speech or any other to help my cause, but only to express my views and assert my convictions. When I am no longer a member of parliament I shall still be a Canadian.

I have already said to my hon. friend that I did not question his sincerity. I know that he is sincere but I cannot share his views. I have been reading remarks which were uttered by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) both in and out of the house. I do not find myself in agreement with what he has to suggest, partic-
ularly when I review the criticism which he and certain of his colleagues have levelled at the government which occupied the treasury benches from 1930 to 1935. In one of his speeches the Minister of National Defence used these words:
The Conservative party in Canada did more to destroy national defence than has been done by any party since confederation.
I do not think that is a fair criticism to make of the attitude adopted by or the work done by the Conservative party since confederation. That criticism is not justified by the conditions which were apparent from 1930 to 1935. We must remember that up to 1936, following the great war, conditions in Canada and generally throughout the world were entirely different from what they are today. There was a period when it was considered out of fashion to discuss armaments or armed forces. The world was striving for peace and for peaceful methods of solving the problems which then confronted it. That condition existed from 1930 to 1935, just as it did from 1926 to 1930. I do not think the government which was in power from 1930 to 1935 should be criticized any more than the government which was in power from 1926 to 1930 as far as expenditures in connection with this particular department are concerned.
Progress reported.

subtopic: PROPOSED SITTING ON WEDNESDAY, MAY 17

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROPOSED SITTING ON WEDNESDAY, MAY 17
speechtext:
Before the house rises for luncheon, may I say that as their majesties will not arrive in Ottawa until Thursday, instead of Wednesday as was originally scheduled, it is proposed to have the house sit on Wednesday. I think this will meet with the general approval of hon. members.
At one o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at three o'clock. SUPPLY

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
General.
208. Adjustment of war claims, $60,000.

Mr. Chairman, when we
closed for the noon recess I was endeavouring to emphasize the fact that conditions, not

Supply-National Defence
only in Canada but throughout the world,
had changed very materially during the past few years, and that I did not consider the criticism which was directed against the previous government or governments, for lack of interest and lack of development in the Department of National Defence, as fair and reasonable criticism. I quote an expression which was used by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie)-an expression which has been repeated many times by other hon. members. I would call the attention of members of this committee to expressions of the sentiment which prevailed, not on the Conservative benches, but on the Liberal benches, between the years 1930 and 1935. For example, when the estimates of this department were discussed in the year 1932, a Liberal member then sitting in opposition was reported as follows:
The budget of this department-
Referring to the Department of Militia and Defence.
-is equivalent to one dollar per capita of the population. More than $260,000 are expended on the League of Nations so as to foster disarmament, while on the other hand millions are expended for military purposes. ... I state that there is no greater waste of money in this country.
The same gentleman in the same debate used words as follows:
At a time of depression, would it not have been more appropriate for the government to leave out this item instead of reducing it?
That is, one of the items in the estimates of the department. Again, another Liberal member, who had been minister of labour in the previous government, used the following words, directed at the Minister of Militia and Defence in the Conservative government:
The government is considering ways and means of saving money, and this vote affords an opportunity to effect a Baving.
The hon. member for Temiscouata used these words in the same debate:
I am pleased indeed to see that this vote has been decreased by three-fourths, but there is still one-fourth left, which might better be nothing. I remember distinctly urging upon the house last year the desirability of giving footballs and baseball bats and boxing gloves to our young boys instead of guns and drums and other militaristic paraphernalia.
No less a person than he who now occupies the position of Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), criticizing these estimates in 1933, said:
I believe it would be better to use this $300,000-
That was an item to be used particularly,
I believe, for cadet training.
-to provide food and shelter for them than to put arms and weapons in their hands.
Colonel Ralston, who had been Minister of Militia and Defence, at that time made this suggestion:
I submit that in view of our economic and financial position this item should be very substantially reduced.
I use these quotations as illustrations of the attitude of the then opposition during the years 1930 to 1935, and to show hon. members that it is not fair for those on the other side of the house to criticize the government of that day for not having done more towards the provision of defence for the dominion. They were criticized by the Liberals then in opposition for doing too much. So why should those same hon. members, now sitting on the treasury benches, suggest that at that time we were doing too little? I have here a quotation from the debate of 1933 in connection with these estimates in which the leader of the opposition, who is now the Prime Minister, used these words:
Certainly the item now before us might well be reduced, and for a year hence could be omitted altogether.
That was the prevailing attitude. And yet, according to the present Minister of National Defence:
The Conservative party in Canada did more to destroy national defence than has been done by any party since confederation.
I do not think that under the circumstances those words are justified. If we did not do more for national defence between the years 1930 and 1935, the Liberal party of that day were just as much to blame as the Conservative party. I have no doubt that the Conservative party acted as they thought best in the interests of Canada, and, because of the peculiar economic conditions, for one thing, kept the estimates of this department at a minimum. But they did so not only because of the economic conditions which then prevailed, but because of the sentiment, which was general in Canada and throughout the world, in favour of peace and a peaceful solution of all problems, national and international.
The ex-minister of agriculture, speaking in the debate of 1934, used these expressions with regard to the Department of Militia and Defence:
How long are we going to keep up these militia districts with all this paraphernalia in every province? I do not think we are con-
Supply-National Defence

fronted with a war in Canada. . . . Are we going on indefinitely with all this business of war preparations?
Following him, the hon. member for Willow Bunch spoke as follows:
I want to join the hon. member for Melville in objecting to this vote. I am one of those who cannot see why, in times like these, we should not reduce this vote for military purposes.
And the hon. member for St. Johns-Iberville (Mr. Rheaume), following, used these words:
I am amazed at the amounts voted for military purposes.
So it seems to me that if there was laxity from 1930 to 1935 in preparations for the defence of Canada, not only should the Conservative government of that day accept the responsibility, but hon. members representing the Liberal party who sat in opposition, and were so strenuous in their objections to the amount of money which was spent at that time, must accept a greater share of responsibility for the condition in which the minister says he found his department when he took hold of it late in 1935. They criticized what was then spent. How much more should they criticize what is being spent at the present time? But I wish to follow that statement immediately with this, that there should be no criticism of the amount requested in this budget, to judge by world conditions to-day and the general sentiment which exists not only in this dominion but throughout the world.
As I was saying, we must face conditions as we find them. We all desire peace. To my mind the surest guarantee of peace is a well armed and well prepared British empire, and a well prepared system of defence on the part of the democracies of the world. In this system Canada must play a vital part. Our attitude, I think, is influenced from three different directions; there are three different influences and conflicting factors in these developments so far as the Department of National Defence is concerned. First, Canada forms a part of the British empire; second, Canada is a member of the League of Nations; and third, Canada forms a part of the American continent. There you have three apparently conflicting interests and we must guide ourselves by due consideration of them. But I would ask this question: To what extent do these interests really conflict? On the surface they appear to be almost contradictory in relation to our attitude, and yet, when we analyse them, they are not. What should we do as regards our position in the League of Nations? My answer would be that we should maintain our position within the league. 
I recognize that to-day it is an impotent agent so far as the peace of the world is concerned, and I say that with some degree of regret, because at one time I did have great hopes for the League of Nations. But, I repeat, it is impotent to-day. Nevertheless we as Canadians and as a nation should continue to give it our support, in the hope that at some time in the future the League of Nations will develop some potency and probably become that factor for peace in the world which we all expected when it was first launched in 1918-20. That is our hope, and in order to assist in the realization of that hope Canada should maintain her interest in the league and help it to develop some potency for major use.
The second point is this. We are a part of the British empire; we accept all the rights and privileges of that partnership, and therefore, in my opinion'-and I speak as a responsible member of this house-while we accept the rights, the privileges and the benefits accruing from our association with the other member states of the British commonwealth of nations, we should also assume our share of the responsibility. And our responsibility as a member of the British commonwealth of nations we can carry out in no better way than by preparing an adequate defence for the people and the shores of Canada.
May I here express my approval of the views recently put forward by the Minister of National Defence. Speaking in one of the western cities he took as his theme the present condition in Canada, which he described as a state of defence-consciousness. I quite agree with him that Canada is defence-conscious at the present time. He went on to point out that in successive imperial conferences certain resolutions had been passed, and he epitomized them in these words: First, that each self-governing part of the empire is primarily responsible for its own local defence. I do not think anyone can take any exception to that suggestion. Second, that the security of the empire is a matter of concern to all its governments. There is no exception there. Third, that the protection of our coasts and seaborne trade in time of war is the responsibility of the government. I do not think anyone can take exception to that. And, fourth, that parliament must consider defence preparations in the light of the financial ability of the public treasury.
In my opinion the Minister of National Defence is carrying out that fourth suggestion to the best of his ability and as he thinks the public treasury will bear the expense he is

Supply-National Dejence
proposing. These statements from the Minister of National Defence are endorsed, I believe, by most hon. members. Certainly, speaking from this side and for myself personally,
I completely agree with what he said on that occasion. We are defence-conscious, and the four definite suggestions he put forward meet,
I believe, with the general approval of the members of this house.
I suggest that we should endeavour to improve existing conditions in Canada from the point of view of the Department of National Defence. I understand that from 1912 to 1914 we were training a militia of between 34,000 and 40,000 men, equipped with Canadian-made rifles, the artillery having the latest type of weapons similar to those of the British army of that day. Last year we did not train more than 25,000 men. The rifles were not Canadian-made and the artillery equipment was for the most part many years out of date. Apparently our position is worse to-day than it was in 1914 in regard to the number of men trained and the equipment at their disposal. I urge that some attention be given to this situation.
We must also take into account the considerable change that there has been in the last few years in mobility and fire power in warfare. To-day both these elements are very much greater than they were in 1914. I read with some interest a speech reported at page 410 of the debates in another chamber and with the remarks of the person who made that speech I am in entire agreement.
I would bring to the minister's attention certain articles, which no doubt he has had an opportunity of reading, published in an old country magazine called Dejence. Therein we find a considerable amount of useful information that could be of practical value to the Department of National Defence. I was also very much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and those of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). These hon, gentlemen put forward very clear and apt suggestions, and in this connection I would say to the minister that nothing commended him more to me personally than his attitude towards those suggestions, coming as they did from members on this side of the house. When the minister crossed the floor for the purpose of complimenting the hon. member for Royal at the conclusion of his speech last night, I regarded this gracious act as a tribute not only to the hon. member for Royal but to the minister himself and a recommendation of his readiness to accept any proposals that might be of practical use in the administration of the department. I am encouraged to
believe that under such circumstances a debate of this kind will certainly have some beneficial effects upon the Department of National Defence.
In conclusion I should like to offer one or two suggestions with respect to the items under discussion. We are asked for a vote of a little more than $63,000,000. My view is that under the circumstances this is inadequate for the defence of Canada under our present conditions. We must have speedy action in placing ourselves in a position properly to defend ourselves and our coasts. Sixty-three millions is little enough; it should be closer to $100,000,000, provided it could be productively spent, as it should be, and as I feel it would be after the lengthy discussions we have had from time to time in this house on defence estimates. I feel that under the circumstances $63,000,000 is inadequate, and I should like to see the amount increased in order to speed action towards a more complete defence than we have at the present time. Of course in spending any such amount of money I urge that we get better than good value for it.
I should like the minister to know also that in speaking as I have this afternoon I believe I am speaking for a considerable body of public opinion in this country which feels as I do-that this matter of defence for Canada is urgent.
I should like to close with this one suggestion. I am sometimes accused of being too imperialistic in my views, but I do not think I am the imperialist that some people suggest. I try to be reasonable in my attitude towards the empire, my attitude towards Canada. We are still a part of the British empire; we are still a nation within the British commonwealth of nations. From that we get certain rights and certain privileges, which we are all glad to accept. And I would go a step further and suggest that with these new rights and new privileges we should also accept our new responsibilities as a nation, a nation within the British commonwealth of nations. For that reason I urge more adequate defences for Canada, because in putting forward these defences we are assisting the empire at large and assisting democracies throughout the world.
The quotation I wanted to use was this:
If Britain be attacked Canada will not be neutral. Canada will stand with and for the empire to which she belongs. She will help defend the people who, she feels sure, would help defend her.
That is my position. Canada, if attacked, Canada, if in danger, wrould rightly feel that she should be able to depend on other parts
Supply-National Defence

of the British commonwealth of nations to come to her succour and defence. Other parts of this great empire, the British commonwealth of nations, should have like confidence in Canada.

I rise at this time to answer some of the arguments made this forenoon by one of the hon. members from Quebec, who quoted from Professor Francis Jehlicka regarding the Slovakian controversy. This man said: "We are neither Czechs nor Czechoslovaks. We are just Slovaks and we intend to remain Slovaks forever."
The problem with which we are to deal is liberty, and if we are going to defend our liberties then these books written before 1938 are out of date to-day. The Munich pact is dead, the treaty of Versailles may have been faulty, but we must face realities as they are to-day. In this great dominion of ours we must preach liberty, and those people who expect to have religious liberty and freedom must realize that in order to retain that religious liberty and freedom in the world to-day they must understand what is meant by British freedom and liberty and attempt to uphold it. Abraham Lincoln said that no nation can live half slave and half free. The chief danger of democracy to-day is ignorance. Professor Laski of London university says that liberty means being faithful to oneself, and it is maintained by the courage to resist. I am not going to speak in favour of large defence estimates with the idea that they will give us courage, because it is the ideal of liberty and truth and courage to live and let the other man live that we must place before our people to-day. Of course we must be prepared with skilled craftsmen, men who will be able to turn out the necessary equipment in case of crisis.
Very shortly we shall be celebrating one of the greatest events in British history. Wherever the English language is spoken, people will bow their heads in token of remembrance of our ancestors who fought for British liberty and obtained from King John the great Magna Charta. Just to-day I received a pamphlet on this subject. What does Blackstone say about the Great Charter? He says:
The Great Charter protected every individual of the nation in the free enjoyment of his life, his liberty and his property, unless declared to be forfeited by the judgment of his peers or the law of the land.
It is in that spirit that I speak this afternoon. I am speaking partly on behalf of my own district, because as I have said before I

realize that my own district presents such a problem in the Canadian economic structure that we wish to make these new Canadians of the west proud of being Canadians.
WTiat have we fought for in the past? We have fought for individual liberty, Magna Charta and British freedom. That is personal liberty. We have fought for our religious liberty of which the hon. member for Port-neuf (Mr. Gauthier) was speaking this forenoon, and I realize that we must have true religious liberty. We have fought for our political liberty, we are fighting for our economic liberty and we must preserve our national liberty at all costs. In this world of ours there are many things which are precious and beautiful. But, wise and learned people, beware lest we lose them. So precious and so beautiful are our liberties, our homes and our spiritual civilization that we must prize and hold them. These things we love; shall we see them destroyed?
An attempt is being made to destroy these things, the very things we hold most dear. It is time for us to stop our dreaming and face realities. Militarism and ruthless force are determined to gain the ripening fruits of civilization by loot and war.
That is why I say the Munich pact is dead; that period of history is over forever and we must face the situation as it is. The promising repiiblic of Czechoslovakia has disappeared from the map of Europe. Why then quote extracts from books dealing with things that happened before that period, when the situation to-day is so different, unless it be to throw light on the subject of how we are to face the situation as it exists? The small adolescent Ukrainian people of Carpatho-Ukraine were given their freedom and liberty for a very short period, and the Slovak people for only one day, when they turned traitor to their own fellow citizens of the Czechoslovakian republic. And what did the citizens of this little Carpatho-Ukrainian state do? Did they give everything to the aggressor? No. To their eternal honour the citizens of this little autonomous state flung themselves into a fight for liberty and life, for hearth and home, against the invader from whom they had been emancipated. The Ukrainians who came to the defence of that small republic were disarmed, and 121 of their people were shot. Would it not have been well for the Slovak people if a hundred of her best citizens had been shot, to form a group of men whose honour would live forever in the hearts of the Slovak people? If anyone wants to take my home he will have to march over my dead body, but unless we are prepared to fight for the things we love we

Supply-National Defence
might as well give up. These Ukrainian peasants had no chance against armies fully equipped with artillery and airplanes. This little republic, whose citizens defended its flag with their blood, has ceased to exist. Among the hundreds of Ukrainian citizens who were killed was Grenja Donsky, their principal writer and poet. May his name live forever 1 This ancient and virile race has now developed a mystic flame of nationalism deep within its people. Their fervent hope and prayer is that their children may be enabled to rise again at least to the level of economic, agricultural and social betterment from which they have now been cast down.
The new rapproachement between the states of eastern Europe which feel themselves threatened by German expansion has developed. Occupation by force, audacity and speed has opened their eyes to the precariousness of their situation. The shadow of the European catastrophe falls on the world again to-day. Nations are working feverishly to increase their defences. What will be the end of it all? We must encourage manufacturing skill, honesty and integrity among our people and among our leaders. We must be true to ourselves.
I should like to leave in the minds of hon. members these words of Shakespeare:
This above all: to thine own self be true,
And it must follow, as the night the day.
Thou canst not then be false to any man.

At the outset of my remarks I wish to compliment the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) upon his able address, both in English and in French. May I say to him, however, as well as to the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hayhurst), that I was impressed with this idea: that if loyalty was to be measured by the expenditure of money for armaments we need not carry this discussion any further; we might as well vote any amount proposed by this or any other government. From the point of view of loyalty no hon. member objected to the motion presented to-day by the leader of the government. We sang God Save the King sincerely; and what we have said and sung in this house is only an expression of the feeling throughout the length and breadth of Canada, which feeling will be shown in the hearty welcome which will be extended to their majesties when they arrive in our country.
We are all loyal. The question is not one of faith in the empire, in the flag under which we live or in the institutions which are ours. Any discussion on these items cannot bring about any real disagreement, any
disruption or any dismemberment. In Canada we are solid as a nation from coast to coast; we can stand shoulder to shoulder to protect our common interests. The question is one of amount, of motive, of objective. Even some hon. members from the province of Quebec do not seem to get at the root of the problem and to face it as they should. The other evening a responsible minister of the crown made use of irresponsible language when he used the words "the saviour of the races" in trying to ridicule some of us who are fighting here in what wTe believe to be a good cause. The Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) has not a monopoly on wisdom. Ministers of the crown, although possessing many heroic virtues, have human frailties; and in this case a great mistake was made. I wish to protest against that form of dictatorship. Speeches against Hitler or Mussolini will not solve anything on this side of the water. The same statement might apply to the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Francceur), who spoke yesterday evening as though he were a school teacher addressing school children, speaking of discipline with a whip in his hand, trying to cast ridicule, speaking of cheap popularity and cheap appeals. This sort of thing will not lead us anywhere. We are here as free men. I am the representative of a riding in which the people are as intelligent as those in any corner of this dominion. I have been told by my constituents what they want. I have received requests, letters, decisions of councils, societies and clubs, and I know what the objective is. Speaking in the city of Quebec some years ago before the Liberal youth of that district the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) said, "Within the ranks of our party there is freedom. Do not be afraid to talk." I am here and I am going to say that this problem should be looked in the face and scrutinized in its proper light.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) understands me very well, I am sure. Not only is he a good speaker and a genial leader; he is also an author, and I had the pleasure of reading his book the other day. In that book he speaks of the ostracism which is the lot of the member who has the audacity to differ with the government of the day or the leaders of his party. This is a matter of duty. I want to point out right now, Mr. Chairman, that there is unanimity on the question of national defence. There is no dispute in regard to proper, reasonable defence, something within bounds, within limits; but we are running away with ourselves. My views are known; I have expressed
Supply-National Defence

them during every session of this parliament, and they have not been changed by what I have heard or by what has been done. Every speech gives an additional argument against the proposals dealt with in these items. We are not dealing with Canada; we are dealing with the world. We are not taking as an objective the welfare of our country; we are trying to save the empire, to save democracy throughout the world. In his speech the last speaker, the hon. member for Vegreville got away from our shores and dabbled in European politics-Czechoslovakia. We are getting involved-
The reason I did that-

We are getting involved in European problems at a time when, apart from military matters in Canada, we have so many local things to do, things which require our attention and our funds.
There are two schools of thought. One is imperialistic and the other is strictly Canadian. We must choose between the two. If you belong to one, well and good. I belong to the second one, because I cannot forget what took place in 1914. Say what you like, we were carried off our feet; we spent money to the point of ruin. Without necessity we sent thousands of our young men to their death. At a moment's notice we became crazy with regard to conscription. To-day we have promises and we are asked to accept the word of this or that public man.
No greater Prime Minister than Sir Robert Borden has existed in Canada. He had his faults, but he has passed on now and his name will live in history. Sir Robert Borden promised solemnly in 1917 that there would be no conscription. He authorized the then Minister of Justice, the Right Hon. Mr. Doherty, to go down to the city of Montreal and promise Archbishop Bruchesi that there would be no conscription, and through that promise managed to get in line the Roman Catholic clergy of a section of my province to appeal to the men to enroll, to pay money and to become interested in war. In spite of those promises, a few months afterwards in this very house through the proposal of Mr. Borden and Mr. Doherty conscription was voted; conscription was established. This did not happen in the middle ages. This is not something that happened in the days of Rome and Greece. This did not happen in Russia. This was not in Spain; it happened in this very building, in this very room, under the leadership of a Canadian Prime Minister.

At that time I was in Alberta, but I know that in Quebec conscripts were treated like slaves. In the very city of Quebec there was bloodshed. The king's soldiers shot down peaceful men on the streets. These things are not forgotten; they live. Every man of my age, or ten or twenty years younger, has in his mind all these facts. And that is why I stand in my place to-day and pray that we may get away from an imperialistic policy -praying, too, that we may get away from any policy that will draw us into a world conflict. We want to attend to our own country, and stay Canadian. Conditions were so bad in 1918 that the hon. member who now represents Lotbiniere, then a member of the Quebec legislature-and I am sorry he is not now in the chamber-presented a motion requesting that Quebec separate itself from the rest of confederation.
The two larger political parties are now agreed that there will be no conscription, that there will be no expeditionary force. Mr. Chairman, I will give my own opinion on the subject. This aspect will change overnight. Agitation or pressure will be brought to bear on us. Last September, when there was a little stir in the old country, we were on the eve of being called to the House of Commons-and I know very well what was going to happen. I know very well what was in the minds of the ministers, the leaders of the different parties and the majority of the population.
If we analyse the arguments which have been presented by some hon. members who have preceded me, it is obvious that the minds of a certain number of members are saturated with only one object. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) said, in effect. "We have commitments; let us cooperate with England-no camouflage- the government should announce its policy in the open." He advocated a tremendous military lay-out, and no limit to expense. Then, the hon. member for Mount Royal, who spoke a little while ago, expressed himself along similar lines. The leader of the opposition, when presenting his side of the case, explained that there was solidarity among the democracies. He congratulated the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) upon the fact that fifty air pilots had been borrowed from the other side-a common viewpoint, and common ideals.
We are not dealing with Canada; we are going beyond the boundaries of Canada, and that is what I object to. I want to limit myself to the requirements of my country, not because I have no love for other countries, not because I have not at heart the

Supply-National Defence
good and the welfare of the motherland and not because I am not interested in democracy as an ideal, or as something to be preserved the world over. But I say that this country, large in size, with tremendous resources, has not the population, has not the social organization and has not the financial standing to go ahead to adopt a program such as is suggested. We should deal with local requirements, and that only.
We are told, as a commonplace, that neutrality is impossible. The statute of Westminster which we bless-I praised it myself in this house-is becoming ill understood. It is meaningless. Our powers are limited. We are not the nation we had thought had come into existence a few years ago. "When England is at war, Canada is at war." The menace is held over our heads. We must fortify-right, left, east, west! Millions must be secured and expenditures must be lavishly made I We are already in the furnace. Potentially we are committed to war-and that is where Canadianism, as I understand it, and as I believe in it, is overlooked and being discarded.
The hon. member for Mount Royal spoke of the attitude of mind. He referred to what the Liberal party had said in 1933, when it objected to too large an expenditure for military purposes. Surely; that is true. And before 1933 we had been objecting to it right along. A right-about-face is taking place just now, and has been taking place, for a year or two. The present government is a convert to imperialism; and that is where I cannot support the increased vote, not so much because of the amount, proper, as because of the reasons underlying the proposal. There is a plan which is honestly and gradually being elaborated and developed. Just three sessions ago the Minister of Justice said that the money being voted then would not be used for war purposes, that it was to protect us against communists. It was to be a purely local proposition, but it is not a local proposition any more. If there was any intention that it would be kept that way, that intention has been discarded.
I do not want to delay the committee any further. I think I have explained my view point, and I hope hon. members of the committee will get away from the idea that there is any disloyalty, that there is any weakening of affection or devotion on my part, I simply say that we are undertaking too much. This country cannot stand it. We have a relief problem in the province of Quebec and in our cities are many men without shelter and without food. There
are men in this condition in my own city. They come to me, but what can I do? Last year the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) gave the province of Quebec a mere pittance of $400,000 a month, or $4,800,000 for the year. Compared with that, we are to provide $60,000,000 for the wheat deficit, another $60,000,000 to take care of our railways, the Hudson Bay railway, the Prince Rupert elevator and other matters. We are eating into the treasury of this country at the rate of hundreds of millions, and we are still not getting rid of our troubles.
We are now being asked to vote millions of dollars more for guns and other armaments.
I do not want anyone to think I have not great admiration for those Canadians who are soldiers. There is a unit of the militia in my own town and I try to take good care of it. I am ready to support their requests when they are within reason, but I do object to hundreds of millions of dollars being spent in this way when they could be devoted to the real needs of this country.
For the reasons I have given, I shall vote against the increase in these estimates. I am sorry to have to differ with the Minister of National Defence. He is a most likeable gentleman, well gifted and well educated. I believe in his honesty of purpose. I am not paying him compliments at this time in order to excuse myself, I am simply speaking my own mind. I have every admiration for him, but I deplore the situation in which he now finds himself. The budget for these purposes is too great at a time when we have an economic crisis which is getting more serious and when our cities are filled with men who are without work and food. Our farmers are going bankrupt and the credit of the nation is being bled almost to exhaustion. At such times we should not be asked to spend these sums for military purposes, and for that reason I am going to stand by the opinion which I expressed at the beginning of my remarks.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to make a speech on the defence appropriations, because I made several in this house on that subject, in particular during the debate on external affairs and conscription. However, I wish to reaffirm my opinion.
As I already said, I would have been ready to vote, without protest and even with enthusiasm, the millions we were asked to grant, had I been given a legal guarantee that they would not be used for the purpose of sending an expeditionary force to Europe.
Supply-National Defence

Since the military appropriations have been increased year after year, I protested against such increases because we did not have the legal guarantee to which I just referred. And I object all the more as it is stated that our neutrality is an impossibility when England is at war and as the house seems to be generally agreed-if we are to judge by the discussions that took place since the opening of the session-upon the necessity of participating in the next war. In consequence, I wish, this year again, when we are asked to vote those estimates, to proclaim my opposition and my protest against the increase for 1939-40.

Mr. Chairman, I hope I may be allowed to make a few points which I was unable to make in my remarks this morning. I hesitate to detain the committee but, as I said before, this is a problem which is vital to our nation and it should not be dismissed with casual attention.
I hope I was not misunderstood when I endeavoured to deal with this problem in a constructive way by making reference to our British connections. I was not arguing against any advantage which might be derived from cooperation with the British war office; I was rather pointing to the dangers which might result from an over-emphasis of any attempt to encrust our defence preparations with purely British-made plans.
The army and navy are famous for their maintenance of tradition, but we know from experience that sometimes danger lies in the maintenance of tradition. I suggest that we learn whatever may be learned to advantage from that cooperation or exchange of ideas and information; that we should adapt these ideas to Canadian needs. I might remind the committee that during the last war the Canadian corps became a really effective fighting unit when they adapted to the Canadian spirit and the Canadian temperament the lessons which *were to be learned from the regular army. That is quite as necessary for defence now.
My point is that the reasonable deduction may be made from the plan outlined by the minister-I notice this deduction was made by an editorial writer in the Winnipeg Free Press-and from the requisitions made by the general staff for equipment, that we are preparing to provide equipment for an army of manoeuvre, much equipment which cannot be utilized strictly for purposes of coastal defence. I argue that that is dangerous at this stage,

that priority should be given to the completion of plans for the defence of our coasts. I point to the fact that howitzers, mortars and light machine guns are not urgent at this moment for the purposes of coastal defence. In any scheme of collaboration with friendly powers-by this I mean the United States and Great Britain-in viewing the matter from that basis, it is important that priority should be given to coastal defence. When we come to the question of collaboration with other nations we must consider whether or not we collaborate by way of the dispatch of an expeditionary force. In my opinion that is not justified on any grounds whatsoever, nor should plans be made to that end, although it appears to be fairly certain that the staff have that contingency in mind. For that reason I referred to the fact that potential enemies now find it possible to establish naval bases in Spain and northern Africa, and from those bases can raid much more successfully British shipping. An expeditionary force, therefore, in my opinion, would become almost impossible. The disposition of the naval forces of the empire would be such as to make it practically impossible to divert naval strength in order to convoy troops across the Atlantic. This becomes particularly difficult in view of the transport of the supplies necessary under the conditions of modern warfare. I think we should remind ourselves that during the last war, according to military experts who, in recent years, have written freely on the subject, we advanced rather too recklessly and too hurriedly in expeditionary force plans, with the result that in the field we had a top-heavy force, a force to which we could not supply reinforcements except by straining the national resources, and for which we could not provide adequate supplies and equipment.
In regard to an expeditionary force I wish to make plain that under the circumstances the preparation for and dispatch of such a force would cripple and undermine our defence measures in this dominion. We could not safely spare five or six hundred thousand men for service abroad without seriously weakening our defence here. That in turn would weaken the empire front-if you wish to place it on that basis-and would thereby weaken any strategy of cooperation for our support and discharge of mutual obligations determined as a result of imperial conferences. Certainly at the same time it would intensify any attempt at direct reprisals against this dominion, for which we would be poorly prepared. We must remember in this regard, now that Great Britain is looking to Canada as being

Supply-National Defence
an important secondary source of material- I am basing these figures on German computations-that it requires eight men to maintain a machine gun in the field; it requires forty men in the factory to maintain a combat tank in the field; it requires sixty men to maintain a pursuit plane in the air. It therefore becomes apparent that, if we deal thoroughly and completely with our defence plan and all it involves, we cannot safely undermine it by withdrawing from defence, and the organization behind defence, men for overseas service.
I wish to refer to the unsatisfactory conditions under which men may be enrolled for service. True it is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said that conscription will not be enforced in Canada. Nevertheless under stress of present-day events those assurances are quite likely to be thrown overboard; and nothing was said at that time of the likelihood of utilizing the existing provisions of the Militia Act, by consent of the Canadian government, permitting the crown or His Excellency the Governor General on behalf of the crown to enable the voluntary enrolment of men in Canada for overseas service. That is a matter which should be canvassed in a most conscientious way at this time to determine just what it involves. In my opinion the promise of no conscription is meaningless if the government permits or inspires recruiting for overseas service. It is clear that for such recruiting the legal mechanism exists in the Militia Act and the Naval Service Act. I think all the plans point to the almost immediate dispatch of air squadrons and possibly naval service units for service abroad. But if such recruiting is permitted with the consent and the support of the Canadian government, we shall rapidly move into a situation where conscription will become inevitable. Such recruiting would immediately inspire a wave of sentiment which would demand the dispatch of an official expeditionary force. Such voluntary recruiting would immediately make it apparent that there was a disorganization or inequitable distribution of service demands. Men inspired by patriotism would leave work essential to war time industry and there would be a general disorganization which could not be coped with under any such plan. Our defence arrangements would be disorganized; and while I can well understand that there would be a natural sentiment abroad throughout the country in support of such action, it would eventually lead to a situation where Canada would have a heavy stake in an overseas expeditionary force. We should be in exactly the same position as that in which we found
ourselves in 1917, when, Canada having 237,000 men in the field, the government was compelled to say: We now have an emergency which demands the imposition of the provisions of the Militia Act-and that act provides to-day, as it did then, for compulsory military service. So that ultimately the emergency would be so apparent as to warrant the imposition of conscription in Canada. Of course, no obstacles could legitimately be placed in the way of those who for their own personal reasons and at their own personal expense desired to serve abroad.
These are real problems which I think should be faced now in a non-partisan way by the proposed special committee of the house.
I wish to associate myself very heartily with the remarks made last evening by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) with regard to the shipment of war materials to potential enemies. It seems to me highly inconsistent that Canada, which is now engaged in a defence effort demanding considerable sacrifices on the part of the people, should be arming potential enemies. That is the direct effect of the shipments abroad of war materials. I do not intend to discuss that, because the matter has been dealt with fully by other hon. members. For a moment or two, however, I wish to refer to -the activities of Japanese interests on the Pacific coast, which I consider are related to the shipment of war materials to Japan.
It seems ironical that when we are erecting fortifications in Stanley park, at Albert Head, on York Island, right under the guns which we are placing there we see vessels passing and carrying concentrates, copper, scrap iron and other materials to arm a power against which we are proposing to defend ourselves on the Pacific coast. Some time ago I raised the question as to what information the government had with regard to -the activities of Japanese interests, having in mind the thought that possibly they are acquiring control of strategic sites on the Pacific coast. Again, it seems to me highly inconsistent that, with the elaborate fortifications there being erected, dummy companies, operating under English names but controlled by Tokyo interests, should be acquiring ore bodies and valuable timber limits, and engaging in various operations at strategic sites which may threaten the efficiency of our defence preparations there.
I am told on reliable authority that a Japanese-controlled firm has acquired the old Tidewater mine, -about eighty miles north of Port Alberni on Vancouver island. Some of
Supply-National Defence

the shares are held by gentlemen such as Nelson Spencer, of Vancouver; 0. F Lundell, of Vancouver; and L. L. McGhee of Vancouver, but the majority of the shares in this company are held by Japanese interests.
Again, as reported-and I questioned the government on that point-the harbour of Sidney Inlet Mining Camp and four other harbours on the west coast of Vancouver island were dredged and preparations made by the construction of tunnels suitable for the storage of oil. Some of this work was done under the supervision of a former Japanese naval captain.
The Louise Mining Company of Vancouver controls the old Iron Duke mine on Louise island, in the Queen Charlottes. In order to get this control the Japanese had to buy nine crown grants. This mine is said to have ore reserves up to ten million tons, estimated at from sixty-five to seventy per cent magnetite, which is very valuable in the manufacture of certain kinds of steel. The shareholders of this company are listed. There are men "fronting" for this company, but again we find that the majority of the shares are controlled by Japanese interests allied directly to well-known and important firms in Tokyo. The Queen Charlotte Timber Holdings Company, Limited, control nearly one billion feet of timber on Louise island; the N. S. McNeil Trading Company, Limited, control six hundred million feet of timber near Port Hardy. The real owner of this timber is the Nisso Rayon Pulp Company, Tokyo, which is controlled by the Nippon Soda Company, Limited. The shareholders are registered at Victoria. While nominally the directors are Englishmen, the control as registered is with the Japanese. The Granby mine has a three year contract signed whereby Mitsui & Company, Limited, and Mitsubishi Shoji, Kaisha Limited have agreed to purchase all the copper Granby can produce, and according to Mr. N. L. Amster, the company's president, the product goes to Japan as fast as it can be turned out.
All these operations have been going on on the Pacific coast, creating dismay in the minds of the people resident there. I submit that they should be thoroughly investigated. I queried the government about these matters, and the return tabled showed that four or five departments simply had no information and did not seem to evince any interest in the matter. If these things are actually going on, the department should be in possession of the information. I submit that the Department of National Defence should take proper steps to deal with this situation in order to prevent a potential

enemy from acquiring strategic sites or engaging in operations which in time of emergency might seriously impair the efficiency of our defences.
One other point should be kept in mind, and that is with regard to the survey of industrial institutions in Canada. The minister reported to the house that a survey had been conducted with respect to several thousand farmers, and I can see no reason why that should not be advanced to take in a scheme of industrial mobilization such as has been prepared in the United States. There should be a definite plan providing for the mobilization of industry and the conscription of industrial management in advance of an emergency with a view also to devising a plan of taxation of wealth which would result in a more equitable distribution of duty and sacrifice. That would be properly a function of the proposed committee, which could review these plans in advance and determine how the burden of service could be placed on the Canadian people in a fair and equitable manner.
With regard to defence, I have never been able to understand why greater consideration has not been given to the training of our youth physically and technically. I would remind the house once more of the words of a former corps commander, the late General Sir Arthur Currie, who said that for our defensive emergencies we would require, not too much equipment, which becomes obsolescent, a skeleton force, and above all well-trained and physically fit youth. These remarks have particular force to-day when we consider the sources from which our defence forces must be recruited. Quite apart from the military and naval activities, Canada should pay greater attention, for purposes of defence as well as for other reasons, to the physical fitness and the technical training of our young men. It will be extraordinarily difficult to build up a defence force quickly enough to meet any defence emergency if we continue to neglect this particular phase of the problem.
One other thought and I am through, and it is with reference to the general public morale. One of the most effective ways of defending democracy is first of all to put our own democracy in order, and that is what I had in mind when I said that greater attention should be paid to the problem of our young men who to-morrow will be required to defend the country. If we neglect this problem too long we may find, when the time comes, that it is too late for them to prepare to make their contribution to the national security. I suggest, therefore, that our affairs

Supply-National Defence
as a democracy should be put in order so that we may be in a position more effectively to defend our democratic institutions. I have in mind again the words of Major Eliot with regard to the general outlook on this problem. In his book, The Ramparts We Watch, he says:
For our own security we do not need, and we ought not to create, instruments of military power, capable of immediate action on land in Europe or in Asia. It is not needful that we should bear such burdens, nor deliberately propose to assume such dangers to our free institutions as might accrue from a great overseas war, requiring as it would the regimentation of every aspect of our national life.
We should recognize the precious gift of geography and natural resources. We should take advantage of our position and not squander those resources on schemes that are far too ambitious for a country of eleven million people, but we should prepare for the emergency which may require Canada to place itself, as it were, in a state of siege, and prepare to procure our munitions and supplies from within. Eor that reason I consider it dangerous to rely so blindly and slavishly on the British pattern of army organization. We are standardizing altogether too much on British types of equipment. I think there should be closer collaboration now with the United States with regard to types of equipment. There should be a fuller exchange of ideas and information, and the Department of National Defence should explore more fully the possibilities of establishing sources of supply in the United States.
A significant sentence occurs time and time again in the departmental reports with regard to equipment requii'ed in Canada, such as anti-aircraft guns, that it has been almost impossible to get delivery. Certainly as the tension abroad increases, the chances of delivery become more remote. If an emergency should overtake us, our supplies will be interrupted from trans-oceanic sources. For our own safety and security with regard to equipment we should explore the possibilities of cooperation with the United States government. That again is a break with tradition which may be challenged for various reasons. I am not a technical expert and I do not know how far we should go in that regard, but as it becomes more and more apparent that there should be friendly collaboration between Canada and the United States in this matter, there should be an exchange of ideas, less reliance upon sources of supply across the Atlantic, and closer cooperation in developing sources of supply for defensive equipment required for coastal defence.
My suggestion, therefore, is mainly this. We do not get the answer to the problems of national defence in bigger and better appropriations for defence. I believe we shall have better defence if we can achieve together, on a non-partisan basis, a more detailed study of the problem of national defence from the strictly Canadian point of view in the first place, and on that basis we may more safely discuss methods of collaboration in defence of democracy abroad.

I have no desire to prolong the discussion; for I believe the situation to be serious enough to warrant giving every assistance to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) in getting his estimates through the house.
There are, however, one or two points as to policy which I desire to mention. Much has been said during the discussion of this question throughout the session with respect to a number of vulnerable points in the Dominion of Canada. I want to add this further point; I believe that if the centre of the empire, which is Great Britain, were weakened or submerged, every component part of the empire would then be vulnerable to attack from at least four or five of the powerful countries of the world. Our responsibility and duty must be clear to all thoughtful citizens. The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Gariepy) made reference to the distress which we have in Canada, and we all agree that we have too much distress. It is true that we have in several provinces a provincial income tax as well, which would add approximately an additional one half to the amount which I have quoted for Canada. In some provinces it is one-third, and I believe there is one province where it is more than half.
I might also deal with the larger incomes, but I do not want to take the time. The important thing to remember is the terrific burden of taxation being borne by the lower income groups of men and women in the old country.
That is only one field of taxation. The problem of taxation has various aspects, and one should survey the entire field in order to make a reasonable comparison. But I make this further point, that in the United Kingdom the citizen, in computing his income, must include rent for his home if he owns it. This makes his tax that much more. Then in the field of motor taxation, a licence for even a medium priced car costs almost $200 there. So that, on the whole, they are carrying a crushing burden of taxation for defence purposes.
The next matter to which I wish to refer is the dominion arsenal at Lindsay, Ontario. Some time ago there was some criticism in the press with respect to the cost of production in this arsenal when it was operating during the war years. I am not going to comment on the costs of production at that time; it would be a long story. But one point I want to make in connection with it is that the cornerstone of that building was laid, I believe, on July 1, 1915, and production started there in 1916. I may be out a year but I think that is correct. We all realize that after a year or two of war the vast majority of the skilled mechanics of this country were either overseas or already remuneratively employed in industry. Therefore it was necessary for a large number of unskilled hands to be taken on. I am sure that factor had a direct bearing upon the costs of production at that arsenal when it was in operation during the war.
I want now to convey to the minister my appreciation for the fulfilment of an undertaking which he gave in the house during the consideration of his estimates last year. The rolling mill and foundry divisions of the plant at Lindsay opened on the first of May. While the full staff in connection with that development has not yet been taken on, still the development is under way. With regard to further development I am encouraged by the statement made by the minister during the discussion of matters affecting his department to the effect that the old objections so

far as operations at Lindsay are concerned have entirely disappeared. I am further encouraged by a letter just received from him in which he states:
I can assure you, however, that in the course of the present year there will be a substantial increase in the utilization of the facilities of Lindsay arsenal.
As regards further developments there, I believe that for a period of years the Lindsay arsenal was entirely reserved as an auxiliary arsenal or a plant for production of small arms and ammunition if the country were actually engaged in conflict.
I want to emphasize this point. I do not believe this or any other government is justified in applying one policy to one arsenal and a different policy to the other arsenal in Canada. I believe we should have one policy which should be applied to both arsenals. The Lindsay arsenal and the Lindsay district had to bear the whole burden of being held for auxiliary production for many years. If we must have a portion of our government arsenals held in reserve for that reason, I think it is only fair that part of that burden should be borne by the arsenal at Valcartier and not entirely by the arsenal at Lindsay. I believe present conditions are such that the government would be fully justified in refitting every department of the Lindsay plant for the production of our much needed requirements. I have never supported the theory that the Canadian government should manufacture munitions for the British government, because I would be afraid of the development of conflict between the two governments. I suggest, again, that we should go ahead and refit the plant completely; then, if there is any part we do not need, we could lease it to some company producing munitions for Great Britain or some other part of the empire. If occasion should later arise when we needed that part ourselves, it would be a going concern; the power could be turned on and we could produce to meet our own requirements.
I have on my desk photographs of this splendid plant at Lindsay. I have shown these photographs to a large number of hon. members, and if any others desire to see them I should be pleased to have them examine the pictures if they will come to my room. I have no desire to delay the passage of the estimates under discussion; perhaps when the minister comes to items 176, 177 and 178 in the main estimates and items 622 and 623 in the supplementaries he will give me further information with regard to the intentions of his department concerning the development of the remaining facilities at Lindsay.

Mr. Chairman, in connection with the defence of Canada there is one point which I think is important but which has not been mentioned. I believe we ought to come down-perhaps " crack down " would be the suitable term- on nazi propaganda in this country. I also believe the statements of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) in regard to the acquisition of properties in Canada for the use of those nations against whom we are arming should be looked into. I do not believe there is a city or province in Canada where nazi propaganda is not being carried on, no doubt some of it begun by people who came from totalitarian states, particularly Germany, but too often carried on by so-called Canadians. Now is the time to check up on these people. If they desire to live in Canada and enjoy the freedom and protection of a democracy, then they ought to be stopped from carrying on propaganda which is weakening the defence of Canada from within. No doubt the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) is well aware, as is every member of the house, that this is the new technique; this is the way they win nations now. In the case of a great number of the nations which have fallen in the last year or so, conquest has been accomplished not so much by war as by constant propaganda carried on within those countries. It is not that I am expecting that to happen in Canada, but even here I believe it has done something to lessen unanimity of opinion in regard to the value of democracy and that degree of freedom and justice which we enjoy under it. So I feel that the Department of National Defence might address itself with a good deal of vigour to the question of nazi propaganda in Canada. It is time we quit hiding every time we heard the word " communist " mentioned by anybody and think carefully about the propaganda carried on in this country by the nazis and those who sympathize with nazism.
It is heart-breaking, not only to me but to every member of this house, that we should have come again to a time when we must talk about spending large sums of money for defence. Just ten years ago now, in 1929, we thought there was a real chance that never again would we have to go through a bath of blood, that the world would never again act in such uncivilized and barbaric fashion. There was real hope we had done that for the last time. No one can discuss the question of Canada's defence and the situation in the world as it is to-day without wondering when we shall ever learn; without wondering whether, if we have another war-and it looks as though this is what we are preparing for- 71492-254
we shall be any wiser at the conclusion of it than we were when we wrote the treaty of Versailles. I have reached the point, as I think a great many others have, where I wonder how much we shall have to suffer before we learn that trying to eternally punish will not get us anywhere. If we had started being wise at the end of the last war, possibly we could have avoided spending the money that is about to be voted.
I should like to say how much I appreciated the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver North, who stressed a point which for a long time I have felt needed stressing, namely, that if we are going to address ourselves to the defence of Canada, it must be in cooperation with the United States. It is really ridiculous not frankly to admit it. We have common coastlines; and if we are going to defend the east coast and the west coast it is only reasonable to expect that it should be in cooperation with the other great nation sharing that coastline. Quite frankly, if we do have a real problem in Canada, that is, an invasion of Canada-for which I do not look-I think we shall have to rely on the United States and ourselves, or perhaps I should put it the other way round and say we shall have to rely on ourselves and the United States. I do not believe Great Britain considers coming to our defence. A great many people would not agree with that, but I believe if the unhappy day of our invasion ever comes, Great Britain will not come to our defence. As a matter of fact we could hardly expect her to defend the dominions, which are spread throughout the world.
If we are going to continue spending very large sums of money, such as $63,000,000- and that is a great deal of money-I think we have to convince the people of Canada that this money is being spent wisely, carefully and perfectly honestly. I do not think anything could have been more disconcerting than the difficulty about the Bren gun. I am not a military expert, but I did not like it, and I think everybody in Canada felt the same way, including the party which is attempting to defend that deal. That there should have been any suspicion-and I do not care how slight it may have been-was most unfortunate, because-
