stress for a moment the fact that it is but a form of hypocrisy to say that we want to defend Canada and at the same time allow powerful interests in this country to go on arming the nations against which we are preparing to defend ourselves. It is not honest; it is not sensible. Either we must stop sending munitions and materials to make munitions to the countries we fear, or look continually foolish to ourselves.
It is such a distorted picture that possibly the less we say about it at this time, the better. But it is perfectly clear that the Canadian government is, with regard to foreign affairs, becoming a mere shadow of the British government. I do think Canadians want to know what we are going to do with this money. Are we going to use it to defend Canada, or are we going to use it in overseas wars which, so far as we are concerned, will be brought about by Great Britain? Frankly I have certainly not agreed with the policy of the Prime Minister of Great Britain. I have felt that I wanted as publicly and carefully as possible to dissociate myself from his policy-not that it would matter to him, but because it would matter to me. The Canadian government has just yes-yes'd the British government in whatever position it has taken. Whether it took one position or another, the Liberal government in Canada, led by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) came out and justified what the British government had done. That is not at all in keeping with other statements which have been made by the Prime Minister to the effect that Canada will decide what we are going to do, and that Canada will decide what our foreign policy is to be. That has not been shown to be true. As I have said, the picture is an extremely distorted one. Those people who were the great peace advocates are those who are most upset by the appeasement policy, and those who were the imperialists have become advocates of appeasement, or peace at any price.
It would take a great deal of time and very careful speaking to try to follow the situation through. I shall not take time at the moment to say more than that in the crisis last September I could scarcely believe that Canada would so enthusiastically support Great Britain. That support certainly was not given democratically, because the Prime Minister, whether with or without the consent of the cabinet was saying what Canada thought with respect to the crisis, when I do not suppose any one person in Canada actually knew what Canada did think-because Canada thought this, that, and the other thing.
[Miss Macphail.)
I am not going to speak any longer with respect to this matter, nor am I going to oppose the national defence estimates. But I do feel we ought to know what Canada intends to do with the money; and, not only that, but having spent it, what does she intend to do with the equipment? Is it to be used to defend Canada, or is it to take part in overseas wars? I would also-well, almost warn the government, to be honest with parliament and with the Canadian people. Whatever it intends to do, let it say so now. Do not let us have a repetition of what occurred during the last war, which was so heatedly referred to-and I can scarcely wonder-only a short time ago by an hon. member from the province of Quebec. The people were misled. They were definitely promised there would not be conscription; but there was conscription, and that one thing has done more to divide Canada than has any other event.
The government has a very grave responsibility, and should be completely frank with parliament, or with a committee of parliament. It should be frank with the people of Canada and state whether it will follow British policy wherever it goes, spend the money of Canada and offer the lives of Canadians to defend British policy, or whether it intends to use the money to defend Canada's shores. Those are very different policies, and, as the hon. member for Vancouver North has said, it is high time we knew which one we are pursuing.

Mr. Chairman, I am a believer in the position taken by nearly all hon. members who have spoken on this subject, namely, that we should endeavour individually to treat it absolutely free from political or partisan viewpoints. Hon. members who have already addressed the committee have shown great restraint and a commendable non-partisan attitude in expressing widely divergent views.
In discussing the estimates of the Department of National Defence I desire now, if I may, to pay a personal tribute. In my view the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), in the perilous times of to-day, is held in high esteem and regard by the great and overwhelming majority of the people of Canada, regardless of political faith -and in my opinion, deservedly so. He came to us from a race outstanding in British history, outstanding in the sacrifice that Scotland has made on the battlefields of empire. He comes to us as a distinguished soldier and a distinguished scholar. For those who believe in strict economy in measures of defence there is the added satisfaction that as a rule

Supply-National Defence
a Scotsman is not profligate with his own dollars or with the dollars entrusted to him to spend. And so from the point of view of the record of a race noted for its courage and noted for its economy where economy is desirable, we are indeed fortunate at this time of our nation's history in having at the helm of the Department of National Defence the hon. gentleman who occupies the position of minister. I congratulate the great province of British Columbia upon having given to parliament and to Canada such a man.
I support the estimates submitted and, speaking for myself only, would advocate an increase in the estimates for two branches of the service.
First, there are the land forces whose task is to protect and guard the vulnerable points of national importance against attack from without and against sabotage from within. I shall deal a little later with the devastation, danger and horror of sabotage by the enemy within our country.
The second branch of the service in connection with which I would favour enlarging the estimates is the air force. I make no apology for repeating what I said to this committee a year ago on March 24 when thf estimates of the air force were under review. I urged that the appropriation of $11,000,000 for that year should be doubled. The estimates for the air force this year are $29,000,000, and I urge this committee here and now to double that appropriation. The reasons why I advocated the doubling of these appropriations a year ago, I believe hold good to-day. Let me put them to this committee briefly.
It should be possible next year to enlist and train 4,000 men for our air service. In the following year we should duplicate this number, bringing the total to 8,000. This would represent a force of 1,000 pilots and
7,000	mechanics, which is the ratio the experts tell us should apply. Our pilots should be trained to operate the highest speed machines that can be turned out. I urged then and I urge now that we should encourage young men who have had practical experience in our garages, young university men and graduates from the schools of science all across Canada to enlist in the air service, either as mechanics or as pilots. The program outlined by the minister and the money set aside for the development of this branch of the service in sympathetic conjunction with civilian flying schools constitute a great step in the right direction.
Let us consider one of the possibilities of the near future. Should a world war become a reality and the things we hold dear be in 71492-2541
danger; should Great Britain and London be bombed, the very existence of the empire would be threatened by extermination. Is there any hon. member bold enough to predict where the front line of defence would be located in such a war? It might well be the English channel. If that should occur, I contend we should make it clear to the world that this country would instantly become involved in such a war. What greater contribution could there be to empire war service and to empire defence, including the defence of Canada, than 1,000 trained pilots with a large number of machines of the high-power type, together with machines of lower velocity, and a mechanical force of
7.000	men to service the fleet?
Could we hope by any other means to make so great a contribution to that ultimate world peace which, I assume, is the desire of every hon. member? It must not be forgotten that such a force as that would have a definite economic peace value. The development of air traffic, both passenger and freight, is in its infancy. Just as twenty-five years ago the first hard-tired, small automobile came upon the scene, the progress in transportation in the next generation will be made in the air. I regret that this type of transportation will also be used for destructive purposes. With a population of 11,000.000 people, Canada cannot hope to compete with the armies of the world. It would be stupidity to attempt to do so. But here is a branch of the service in which we can compete, and when I say that I speak from the record of the last war. By common consent, even on the part of our enemy, Canadian pilots and mechanics outshone the pilots and mechanics of every other nation. That is a well established fact.
Let me lay this view before those who lean toward the pacifist viewpoint, and before those who would prefer to have minor rather than increased contributions made at the present time. There is a selfish aspect which may be considered in the creation of an air force such as I have outlined. A force of 8,000 men, made up of 1,000 pilots and 7.000 mechanics, would in my judgment-I have verified this by conversation with one of the greatest airmen of the world, a distinguished Canadian-be of as great value in war-time as
200.000	men in the infantry, cavalry and other branches of the service.
Let me say a word to my hon. friends from Quebec. Personally I have the greatest regard for the province of Quebec and its people. I number among my warmest and most cherished friends Canadians of French descent both in and out of this house. I have a most

profound admiration for the French-Canadian people of Quebec and I have a most abiding faith in their loyalty to the British empire. Let me say to those who entertain genuine doubts as to the wisdom of the expenditures we are now discussing that they should have no false notions as to the type and character of the enemy who threatens the existence of our empire and our Canadian national life. He is the avowed and implacable enemy of religion and particularly of the Roman Catholic religion. The philosophy of life of the leader of that enemy is recorded in his book " Mein Kampf." I should like to quote from page 377 of Hitler's book as follows:
The sole earthly criterion of whether an enterprise is right or wrong is its success.
This is the creed of the German gangsters. Then listen to what Doctor Goebbels had to say at Stuttgart on September 4, 1938:
The methods by which a people forces its way upwards are of no moment; only the goal which is reached is important.
What do we, the people of a nation who thought the golden rule counted for something, think of a doctrine of that type? What do hon. members think of the philosophy of an enemy who puts forward such expressions as that to the youth of his land? Notwithstanding the perils from air attacks by way of Hudson bay and James bay, which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) outlined so ably yesterday, as a possible menace to Ontario, Manitoba and the prairie provinces-
And Quebec.

I had overlooked Quebec. In my opinion British Columbia, Quebec and the maritimes are in greater peril to-day than are the central parts of Canada including the province in which I reside. If that be so, then these estimates are of greater importance and offer more protection to British Columbia and Quebec and the maritimes than to the rest of Canada. Notwithstanding that, surely all true Canadians must view the defence of our country as a whole and be ready to make cheerfully their individual and provincial contributions. Why do I say that Quebec is in greater peril than central Canada? Let me remind my hon. friends from Quebec of the history of the great war, of the ruthless and cruel bombing by Germany of those magnificent cathedrals and churches at Rheims, Ypres and Albert. They were the special targets and were destroyed from the air, notwithstanding their classic and historic beauty, the result of centuries of art and culture, and the sacred shrines of worship dedicated to humanity and to her people by the Roman Catholic church. The hatred and venom of the Germany of 1914 have not been abated by the

madman of Germany of to-day. Of all the ruthless persecutions within Germany, except that of the Jewish race, the persecution of the Roman Catholic church has been the most cruel and venomous. Her sacred and holy orders have been ruthlessly disbanded and suppressed. The pulpits of her cathedrals have been silenced. Her priests, scholars and religious leaders have been arrested, persecuted and imprisoned. The youth program of that church has been strangled.
I say to the people of Quebec: You cannot expect this German leopard to change his spots; and if it ever comes within his power to enter and destroy this fair country of ours, you of the province of Quebec may expect to become a special target of the hatred and destruction dictated by a mind steeped in cruelty and revenge. Not only your great industrial plants, but your beautiful shrines, cathedrals and churches in Quebec and Montreal and dotted across your province-all these will be regarded as obstacles in the way of German kullur and be ruthlessly removed. You have developed in Quebec more water power plants for industrial purposes than has Ontario or any other province. Your plants, including the great Beauharnois, the Mae-Laren Quebec, the Gatineau and many others, produce 3,800,000 horse power. Your cities of Montreal, Quebec and other centres have great industrial plants which would be vulnerable, and which are vulnerable to-day to an enemy from within.
The danger to-day in the event of war breaking out in which the empire or Great Britain became involved is not merely from without this country. I base that statement on the actual record of German conduct in the last war. Few people in Canada appreciate what the German high command did at that time in the destruction on this continent of property, plants, foodstuffs, war supplies, arms, munitions and ships-all their activities being cunningly planned and financed from Berlin. Let me make clear, before I give this ghastly record, that there are in Canada today a very great number of foreign-born and Canadian-born British subjects of German, Italian and other nationalities who are absolutely loyal British subjects and loyal Canadians, and who are not and must not be taken to be included, directly or indirectly, in any indictments which my remarks may contain. On the other hand there are in Canada to-day-and reference has been made to the fact passingly in this discussion-certain subjects of the foreign countries I have indicated who are enemies within our bosom, who are prepared to destroy our country from within, and who, if the history of the last

war and the known facts and lessons connected with it are to be relied upon, will be equipped with money, leadership, brains, dynamite, bombs and poison serum for the express purpose of paralyzing and destroying our contribution of supplies and man power in the next war. It is the duty of those in charge of this country and the duty of every loyal citizen to be tremendously alert and to cooperate in the necessary governmental and military agencies and through the necessary citizen agencies to counteract the campaign of espionage, sabotage and treachery to which this country will be deliberately subjected from within in the event of war.
A counter-espionage service in Canada cannot be created over-night. Its efficiency depends upon such factors as these: first, an experienced personnel; second, the possession of accurate records of suspects; third, the watching of those suspects; fourth, the piecing together of information obtained from all parts of the country; finally, a swift and firm-moving government bureau to carry out a policy of arrest, prosecution, imprisonment and deportation of "our enemies within."
We have passed an Official Secrets Act. That will help to some extent. Great Britain in the last war had a superb secret service which extended to every country in the world. Her secret service agents operated in the United States and Canada during the period when German sabotage activities were carried on to an hitherto unbelievable extent in the United States. Prior to April 6, 1917, when the United States declared war on Germany, the British secret service rendered great assistance to both the United States and Canada. But the efficiency of the secret services of both the United States and our own country should be a lesson to us not to be caught unprepared again. Let me, without comment as to its justification or lack of it, relate what Germany did in that regard in the last war. Hon. members will ask themselves whether in the next war we may expect her to be less aggressive, less cruel, less ruthless, less unscrupulous. For my part I cannot be persuaded that she will be. If there be any choice in that regard, I would fear that we may expect greater cruelty and ruthlessness, if that be possible, under the present high command than even under that which operated in the last war.
Shortly after the outbreak of the war Germany instigated and equipped a campaign of sabotage, of dynamiting, destruction and international murder by placing a large sum of money in the hands of-whom? In the hands of her diplomatic representatives then residing in the United States. On the
surface they were there to carry out their diplomatic functions and to preserve friendly relations with the United States. Surreptitiously they were there to direct German sabotage activities, which they did. Count von Bernstorff was German ambassador at Washington. Captain Franz von Papen was immediately established with headquarters in New York city at 60 Wall street as the bureau of the military attache. He is now Hitler's ambassador to Turkey. If to-day's news be true, he is not as clever as he used to be, and his mission has been somewhat of a failure, because we hear that there is now at least an understanding between Turkey and the motherland. Captain Boy-Ed located himself at 11 Broadway. Doctor Albert, another high official, opened quarters at 45 Broadway. One hundred and fifty million dollars in German treasury notes, according to Doctor Albert's later admission, were immediately brought into the United States for use, among other purposes, under the innocent looking title, "Stopping munitions for the allies, necessary propaganda-and other things." I am quoting the language of this admission of the German official himself.
Owing, sir, to the wonderful and early activity of the British secret service in obtaining and decoding German secret service messages, the following telegram was caught early in the war. The German general staff at home telegraphed the German embassy in Washington via the foreign office. From the following message I quote:
For military attache. You can obtain particulars as to persons suitable for carrying on sabotage in the U.S. and Canada from the following persons:	one, Joseph MacGarrity,
Philadelphia, Pa.; two, John P. Keating, Michigan Avenue, Chicago; three, Jeremiah O'Leary, 16 Park Row, New York.
One and two are absolutely reliable and discreet, number three is reliable but not always discreet. These persons were indicated by Sir Roger Casement. In the U.S. sabotage can be carried out in every kind of factory for supplying munitions of war.
Zimmerman.
The following almost unbelievable list of dynamiting atrocities were carried out by this gang and their tools and agents. Many of these tools and agents were afterwards caught, convicted and served prison terms in the United States, and from many of them confessions were obtained.
May I be pardoned if I cite part only oi the successful operations of this gang? In every instance supplies and munitions for the allies were destroyed. If I might have the permission of the committee I should like to put the list on Hansard. It is so long that I hesitate to read it. It would save time if I could put it on the record.

For the moment I might refer to two or three of them. On January 1, 1915, there was an incendiary fire at the Roebling plant in Trenton; on January 3, 1915, a mysterious explosion on the SB. Orton in the Erie basin; February, 1915, an attempt to blow up the Vanceboro bridge on the Canadian Pacific railway between Maine and Canada. Werner Horn, a German reserve officer, was arrested and confessed.
On December 12, 1914, the following cipher telegram, No. 357, was sent from Berlin to von Bernstorff:
Secret: The transportation of Japanese troops through Canada must be prevented at all costs if necessary by blowing up Canadian railways. It would probably be advisable to employ Irish for this purpose in the first instance as it is almost impossible for Germans to enter Canada. You should discuss the matter with the military attache. The strictest secrecy is indispensable.
This was followed on January 3, 1915, by a second cipher telegram to the ambassador:
Secret: The general staff is anxious that vigorous measures should be taken to destroy the Canadian Pacific in several places for the purpose of causing a lengthy interruption of traffic. Captain Boehm who is well known in America and who will shortly return to that country is furnished with expert information on that subject. Acquaint the military attache with the above and furnish the sums required for the enterprise.
Werner Horn pleaded guilty to blowing up the international bridge at Vanceboro, Maine, and was sentenced to the federal penitentiary at Atlanta, Georgia.
Another bomb plot prepared against Canada in the United States at the instigation of the attache was an attempt to blow up the Peabody Overall Company's factory in Walker-ville, Ontario. The German-Washington authorities operated through an agent, Kaltschmidt, who was paid $25,000. They used a willing tool named Lefler, who planted dynamite and attached a time clock. At the same time they set another charge in the rear of the Windsor armouries in which Canadian troops were billeted. The factory bomb exploded; the one at the armouries failed to go off. Lefler was arrested and confessed.
The German-Washington authorities then switched their activities against Canada to the German consul-general in San Francisco, by name Franz von Bopp. This plan was to blow up the tunnel on the Canadian Pacific between Revelstoke and Vancouver, and $3,000 was paid to a tool, Koolbergen, for the job. The tunnel was too well guarded, and the plot failed, but Koolbergen confessed and went to prison.
[Mr. Slaght.l
Early in the fall of 1914 a plot to blow up the Welland canal was formulated by von Papen. The idea was to hold back Canadian supplies and troops destined for France. The scheme had to be abandoned, however, because the canal was too well guarded.
Following the German headquarters' instructions contained in the telegram of January 13, 1915, stating that the " General staff is anxious that vigorous measures should be taken to destroy the Canadian Pacific in several places " a scheme was devised to employ Hindu coolies in the Canadian northwest to dynamite Canadian bridges and tunnels, and von Papen personally paid Schulenberg $4,000 to buy a ton of dynamite and fifty rifles to shoot any Canadian guards in the way. Schulenberg bought the dynamite and arranged the plot, but learning of a leak he got cold feet and fled to Mexico City. Arrested later, in December, 1917, and broken down in health, Schulenberg confessed the details of the plot.
The Canadian Car and Foundry Company, Montreal, whose president at the time, since gone, was my good friend W. W. " Ben " Butler, well-known to many hon. members, well-known to the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Cahan)-
He was not the president; he was then an official.
He was later president, perhaps.
Later.

He had obtained a very large munitions contract from Russia, one of our allies, and established a shell-manufacturing plant near Kingsland, New Jersey. The contract was for 5,000,000 shells at a price of $83,000,000. On January 11, 1917, the plant was blown up, and for four hours a bombardment of high explosive shells rained down. The whole plant was ablaze. The entire plant was destroyed and the loss was $17,000,000. To that extent Russia and our allies were short of munitions. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, one of the directors of the company-

I have spoken longer than I had intended; but let me expose my purpose in troubling this committee with these details. It is fourfold:
First, to expose the perfidy of double dealing by a nation who under international ethics were compelled to respect the confidence and honourable manner in which they were treated by the foreign country in. which they were situate, and used that international honour privilege as a means to destroy property and life, while at the same time dining at the White House and breaking bread1 and drinking wine with the leaders of the nation whose property and people they were destroying with dynamite and bombs.
Second, to warn the people of Canada that we may expect at the present moment to find within our midst a powerful, destructive force of secret service German agents, ready to operate against our property and the lives of our people should war with Great Britain become a fact.
Third, to bespeak the Canadian people to be alert, watchful, aggressive and communicative with headquarters against every suspicious subversive activity of which special knowledge may come to them.
Hon. members may have recently seen in Toronto and elsewhere agitations for a commission to investigate nazi activities and communism. In my view we might almost as well ring the bell and expect the secret service agents to come forward and surrender, as to hope to get anywhere by commissions of that kind with public sittings. We have a magnificent secret service force in Canada, but it is all too small-I say that with great respect for the Minister of Justice (Mr.. Lapointe)-at the present moment. His estimates for the upkeep of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police will come before the committee ; they amount to six million dollars odd, and it is not my purpose to discuss-them at this moment. Because we stinted our money contribution for a preventive service, we may have subversive elements in this country, who are able to go into Quebec or Ontario or anywhere else in Canada and destroy some of our great power plants, which could not be replaced in less than one or two or three years at best. That would paralyze the industry of this dominion. In my humble judgment we must take steps to provide our departments with sufficient money now to prevent those things happening, because the money required for such purpose would not be relatively great compared with even the .$63,000,000 that we are now voting. I believe that is the greatest insurance, the best protection both to ourselves and to the empire that we can possibly conceive at the present time.
I have given three of my purposes in introducing this subject at this time; I will conclude with the fourth. It is to arouse public opinion as to the character and tactics of the German high command, who are the product of a cruel and ruthless philosophy which I have described to the committee, and who in my opinion do not in that respect represent the real or true character of the better element of the great mass of the German people.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not think we should be unduly aroused by the spirited speech of the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght). I was in London in December, 1914, and as the old law firm of which I had been a member were the law agents of the war department and the admiralty in Canada and elsewhere in America, I was asked by the war office to undertake certain services in the United States. I was in their service until nearly the end of 1917, so that I personally saw a great deal of the work of the British secret service and the German secret service in the United States. I then returned to Canada, late in 1917, at the request of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice, and assumed a position which was called director of public safety in Canada. Then I was in close cooperation with Colonel Sir A. Percy Sherwood and the dominion police forces under his charge, and subsequently, after Sir Percy's retirement, with his successor. I have a store of copies of public documents and official reports and others which I obtained during that service. I may write it up some -day, when I have nothing else to do, in my autobiography.
Not while you are in the house.

I came back to Canada as director of public safety, and I must say, with firm conviction, that I found the dominion police force at that time thoroughly efficient and adequate to deal with all the alien conspiracies that were attempted in Canada. That force did splendid service, and there were no German conspiracies which were successful under the dominion police force in Canada. I have no doubt that, under the Minister of Justice, the dominion police, now the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, is quite as efficient to-day as it was then, so I doubt whether we should feel unduly alarmed by the statement of the hon. member for Parry Sound this afternoon. That statement may serve a useful purpose, but the people of Canada can rely upon this, that if the dominion police force, now the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, is as efficient now as it was in 1917 and 1918-and I believe it is even more efficient-it will be able to take care of the German secret service and control its manipulations in Canada in case another war arises. I am confident of that.
Some day I shall have to take from storage some of these documents which are now deposited in a large safe in Montreal, where I keep them safely, and amuse the public by publishing some real detective stories, dealing with my personal experiences in those years. I saw the British secret service at work in the United States for several years, as I was more or less counsel with them in some important matters. I will say, however, that I do not believe there was any police force in the British empire more efficient than the dominion police force during the later years of the war.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make it very clear that I intended to pay a tribute to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I know something of their work; I believe they are as highly efficient as any force in the world, and I think it would be most unfortunate if anything I said should be construed as indicating that I have any other view.
I did not suggest that.

To
anyone coming from British Columbia, Mr. Chairman, the question of defence naturally suggests naval defence, the necessity of defending our shores against a naval attack. I had not intended to say anything during this debate, but some remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) suggested an opportunity once more to press upon the government a matter that is very close to my heart and that is increasingly, and
Supply-National Defence

to a surprising extent, becoming the subject of discussion and deep interest in my province. People whose occupation and residence apparently would militate against taking any interest in the matter are taking up the subject.
The hon. member for Vancouver North mentioned one or two instances of the infiltration of subjects of a certain Pacific power into British Columbia. There have been several instances of this within the district which I represent. I know the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) fortified a certain island on a channel which would be one of the natural approaches to the city of Vancouver. It is within my knowledge also that a certain headland, consisting of a considerable acreage only a few miles away, has been taken over by the nationals of a foreign power, for no particular apparent reason. I know of timber limits taken up as such which anyone with the most superficial knowledge of timber would condemn as timber limits; and we know of copper mines being taken up in the way the hon. member mentioned. So we wonder if there is some association in these matters. We know also that this nation has a large body of fishermen on the west coast; and there have been instances in which some of those apparently ordinary fishermen, clad in the rough working garb of their calling, have been identified by some of the prominent men in our own naval services as being men who were high in the naval service of this other country.
I desire to give, credit to the Minister of National Defence for having two years ago inaugurated a naval reserve of working fishermen on the Pacific coast. Perhaps he was instigated to do so by his knowledge of how well that system has developed, and to what a large extent it is practised, in connection with the British navy. I had a notice of motion on the order paper suggesting the same thing. The government did not allow me to bring it forward, but the minister was kind enough to tell me that he already had the matter in mind, and since that time he has taken this action. At the present time that reserve consists of only a few hundred fishermen, but there is every possibility- and I have no doubt it is the intention-of extending it. I believe the results have been splendid. These men are the very finest class of what you might call naval reservists for the job you want them to do. In the operation of a mosquito fleet, and for service of that kind, they are probably even better than men trained on a man of war. They are familiar with every bay and channel on both

Vancouver island and the mainland, a coast line covering thousands of miles in all. Not only do they know every bay and channel; they also know every rock and shoal. As members of a mosquito fleet, as scouts, as pilots, as mine layers or mine sweepers in time of war, these men would be almost worth their weight in gold. The reserve is still comparatively small; the men are trained for some weeks in the slack fishing season, but they form a valuable nucleus.
But, Mr. Chairman, there is a dark shadow over the future prospects of our naval reserve on the Pacific. What is the minister's own colleague doing in this matter? He is undoing the good work the minister has spent time, money and energy in promoting. He is permitting and, more than that, inviting the extension of a system which will eliminate this valuable class of hardy fishermen so familiar with our western shores. Last night in the mail I received' a copy of a resolution passed by the youth council of British Columbia, who have made such extraordinary progress in recent months that they now claim to represent over 45,000 of the youth of that province. They passed a number of resolutions dealing with various matters, including one dealing with the subject I am discussing. I shall not take time to read it all, but they concluded by saying that it was the considered opinion of this large body of the youth of British Columbia, most of whom could have no personal interest in the fishing industry, that the continuation of fish traps in British Columbia was highly inimical to the interests of that province.
Order.

And I would go further
than that and say, inimical to the interests of Canada as well. I imagine my hon. friend is going to suggest that this matter is already under consideration by a committee and that therefore I should not mention it. That objection might be considered well taken; but there are moments when the consideration of matters of vital importance compels even a law-loving man like myself to break a formal rule rather than pass by an opportunity to do something for the good of the province from which I come and the empire to which we belong. I will put it this way, to meet the objection of my hon. friend; I will say that apart from the increased employment which would result, a substantial and extremely inexpensive aid to our defence scheme on the Pacific coast would be created if those traps were done away with. In that way we would guarantee the maintenance not only of the fishing

industry but of some 12,000 fishermen who now make their living in that industry, ninety per cent of whom will be eliminated if the traps are continued. You cannot get much loyalty or protection in time of war from a fish trap, which is a lot of piles and wires.

point of order.

In time of war these 12,000
men will be of vital importance to us.

Mr. Chairman, I do not believe in war, and I make no apologies for my attitude in that regard. Yet I must congratulate the minister and his department upon increasing Canada's protection. There was a statement made by the Prince of Peace, which I think has been grossly abused-"Whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." I think alongside of that should be placed another statement of the same Prince of Peace-"Neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you." I know from my own experience with volley ball that one must be able to take care of himself, and be in good shape to do so.
The cape at Thunder bay is a vulnerable place. We have, if not the bread basket of the world, at least an important storage point. In that vicinity are thirty of the biggest elevators to be found anywhere, comprising the greatest elevator system in the world and the greatest grain handling equipment. That system should be protected, and I suggest two ways of doing so.
71492-255J
First of all, our youth should be trained in a non-permanent force. I say that because the youth in Fort William and Port Arthur are second to none in Canada. They have shown that by their action in the athletic field and by their ability and brilliancy in the university. As an instance I know of a young non-Anglo Saxon who struggled against going to camp for $5 a month, who entered university, earning every cent of the money for his tuition fees, and put himself through university without financial assistance from anyone. He is now a graduate engineer, and a credit to Fort William.
When I think of the accomplishments of athletes at the head of the lakes I am convinced they are fit to take care of all-comers, whether they be from the north, south, east or west. I appreciate the attitude of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) in striving to protect our country in time of emergency, and I am right with him in that regard. I was denied the privilege of going overseas in the 13th field battery, because we had taken to our home children whose mother had passed away and whose father was overseas. The commanding officer of the battery told me I was every kind of a fool, and that I would lose my command if I went to the city of Winnipeg. I do not believe any good can come out of war, but I am convinced we should protect ourselves.
I am convinced another type of armament is absolutely necessary, whether we be in uniform or out of it. I refer to moral rearmament. I was pleased to note that emphasis was laid upon that type of armament by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght). In Fort William we have an air field, and in Port Arthur a water landing place and a splendidly equipped aeroplane plant. Planes are being turned out for use in training. I am sure we will receive from the Department of National Defence the help required to train our youth, and we shall then be able to take on all-comers.

Mr. Chairman, I am absolutely in favour of the defence program, and associate myself with hon. members who have said that in view of world conditions to-day our expenditures are not sufficient. In my opinion what we are doing is a step in the right direction.
A couple of years ago I stated in the house that orientals could land on the Pacific coast and take command of the railway, dry dock and elevator facilities, if they used only a row boat, two men and a machine gun. We could not have defended our coast at that time. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) has realized the strategic
Supply-National Defence

position of the Pacific coast and has at least tried to develop defence facilities. It is ridiculous to think that we should allow outsiders to defend our ports. It was our good fortune to have the benefit during the last war of defence by the greatest fleet on the seas. But in times such as these, can we depend upon that defence? I am pleased to associate myself with the Minister of National Defence who has seen fit to show the world that in a small way we are trying to help ourselves and not depend upon other nations for support.
One suggestion has been made to me, and I believe to many other hon. members, in connection with the awarding of war contracts for the Department of National Defence. I am not criticizing the department for making contracts on a cost-plus basis, but it has been suggested it would be in the interests of the Canadian people and would stimulate greater cooperation if the Department of National Defence were to follow the procedure of other departments and where possible let contracts by open tender. The department might well take that suggestion into consideration. Of course there might be contracts of such a nature that every Tom, Dick and Harry should not be allowed to do the work. The suggestion is, however, that wherever possible the Department of National Defence [DOT]hould follow the practice of the Department of Public Works, and other departments of the government, of letting contracts by open tender. If it were indicated that the Department of National Defence were favourably disposed in that regard, it would assure the Canadian people that there is nothing wrong. I am convinced there is nothing wrong in the department, but when a department finds it necessary to let a contract on a cost-plus basis it is sometimes difficult to convince some people that it has been properly let.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Chairman, just a word. I have listened to some of the speeches, and I agree fully with what was said by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) with regard to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). Before this it has been my pleasure to speak well of his deputy. But, sir, there is one thing not well known outside of the province of Quebec, and that is the real feeling in that province. Of course the hon. member for Parry Sound may have read about the opinions of people in Quebec. I know he was in earnest when he made the statement he did about the people of our province. The people of the province of Quebec, French Canadians and others, are loyal citizens of their majesties. They have no
rMr. Hanson.]
bad feeling toward their fellow citizens. On the other hand, there is one thing that should be understood. They love their country very deeply. First, they love the place in which they live, whether it be city, town or hamlet; then they love their province, and then they love their country. To the great surprise of a gentleman from the United States who was conversing with one of the brilliant journalists in Montreal, a president of the press gallery during the war and a French^Canadian, he was told that no French-Canadian would have any objection to taking up a gun and fighting the enemy in British Columbia or in the maritimes. The French-Canadians look upon Canada as their country. They are ready to defend their country, but they think that the best way to do that is to concentrate our military forces in this country. That is the view of the people of my province. If the hon. member for Parry Sound has not the leisure to make a visit to our province, I invite him to come with me to the press gallery and discuss this matter with some of the prominent French-speaking journalists. I am sure they will tell him exactly the same thing.
I should like to be a pacifist, but it is rather hard because of the many requests I receive from young men in my constituency to enlist in the Royal Canadian Air Force. I doubt if the deputy minister has received more recommendations from anyone else than he has from the member for Temiseouata. I should like to see peace all over the world, but I know there is a fascinating career for young men in aviation and I cannot do otherwise than recommend them without distinction of party. The medical examination and other tests are severe, and I recommend any young man from my constituency who wants to be recommended. A number of those I recommended received appointments in the royal Canadian navy, and I have been told by the officials of the department that these young men are doing quite well.
I want to tell the minister, the officials of the department and the members of the committee that the province of Quebec is far from being disloyal. They do not beat the drum and wave the flag except when it is necessary. They are Canadians, they love their country and are ready to defend it, but they do not want to go outside their country. They think we have enough to do to defend our own country without embarking on what the Minister of National Defence described in an interview which was flashed across the Atlantic as European Machiavellianism.
I do not believe in the European diplomacy of the present time. I do not believe in the Chamberlain government. I do not believe in the intrigues that are now occurring in

Foreign Propaganda
England. I do not believe that French-Canadians or English-speaking Canadians should go to Europe to fight over Danzig. God forbid that we should ever have to live under a rule similar to that which exists in nazi Germany or fascist Italy. I believe in democracy, but I do not believe we have democracy here. I do not believe we have freedom of speech in this house. There are things here that should be looked after right away. Our democratic institutions are being undermined by an abominable bureaucracy. We should start cleaning up at home. We should put order in our legislation, in our government, in the service and in the country. That is my humble view.
We should start at home to defend our country. We should see that our country is defended and we should be most careful about the intrigues and the deceptive diplomacy of European countries. The surest way of maintaining our ties with other British countries is to show the world that we are through with the League of Nations. The League of Nations is responsible for most of the trouble now occurring in Europe. It was conceived by men who had not the ability to make a treaty that would last. The League of Nations is a farce, and I submit that the money now voted for the league should be used for the defence of this country It would thus serve a much better purpose.
